The John W. Mudd M.D. Memorial Western Clinical Psychoanalytic Meeting. San Diego, California. October 11-13, 1991

DELPHINIUMS BLUE AND GERANIUMS RED: DISAGREEMENTS, IMPASSES AND PROBLEMS OF COMMUNICATION IN THE ANALYTIC SITUATION. Theodore J. Jacobs, M.D.

At the first gathering of The Mudd Memorial Meeting, Dr. Jacobs presented a candid discussion of disagreements between patient and analyst, which demonstrated how a careful examination of the analyst's role in their development can be a powerful stimulus to analytic progress. Resistance on both sides of the couch can lead to impasses. Important issues, often unconscious, are concealed in a collusion to avoid painful affects, but rarely discussed is the phenomenon of conscious avoidance by the analyst. Dr. Jacobs pointed out how analysts protect themselves from having to deal with powerful affects and petty faults by focusing on the patient's material. They are adept at creating an analytic screen to deflect painful situations away from themselves. "[We are using] our skills to produce the illusion that we are doing effective work and [to avoid] an uncomfortable truth: that our shortcomings, whether they take the form of a lapse of attention, an unnecessary critical comment, a failure to recognize the truth of a patient's perception, or a momentary need to upstage him, exert a powerful influence on all that occurs at any given time in the treatment situation." The analyst's normal self-esteem needs are at work here. The problem goes beyond countertransference and becomes an issue of human frailty, to which no analyst is immune.

Dr. Jacobs presented two clinical examples describing his attempt, both consciously and unconsciously, to protect his self-esteem, which skewed the analyses.

DISCUSSION: Dr. Jacob G. Jacobson pointed out that "our struggles over rigidity versus flexibility of technique are not new." A departure from the teachings of Freud and our mentors can be lonely and frightening. It is difficult to know when the interpretive path is correct or when it feels like a repetition for the patient of his or her parents' narcissistic needs. If we vary the things we do to maintain the viability of the analytic process, then we will make mistakes. "But," said Dr. Jacobson, "the experience of most of us seems to be that errors made in good faith are seldom irretrievable." He pointed out that it is important to conceptualize our responsivity so that we can understand the difference between facilitative and interfering interventions. Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Upon reviewing her case material, the author concludes that the analyst's memory is very different from the frequent cartoon caricature of the analyst taking notes. The memory does not depend on notes, but as Freud commented, it arouses incredulity along with surprise. It is dangerous if the analyst abuses it for seduction or domination in a fantasized fusion through hypermnesia that submerges the patient in the analyst's omnipotence. The analyst's interventions, in a simplified scheme, could be regarded as a phallic representation, and the analyst's memory as a maternal bosom, attentive and anticipatory. But this bosom could become a prison if the analyst's memory is infallible.

Daymas-Lugassy illustrates the latter notion with a clinical example of a patient whom she had originally seen as a young child, and who returned for analysis as a young adult. This patient had the fantasy that the analyst retained total memory of his earlier treatment, for which he himself had no memory at all. For this patient the analyst's memory seemed to be an auxiliary ego for his childhood self and a guarantor of truth. Thus she emphasized not exact memory per se, but generative or creative remembering in construction of the myth that constituted his treatment.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

The author discusses the emergence of the personal myth in treatment insofar as it focuses the countercathexes of the patient as well as those of the analyst. Her interpretation of the personal myth differs from that of Kris, who thought that the representations repressed by the personal myth could be recovered in the course of an analysis and that the history of the patient, in a sense the patient's autobiography, could be reconstructed. Potamianou feels that there is no such "truth" to reveal, for the imagination of the individual never ceases to infiltrate the reality of events. The notion of an objective reality to recover is nothing but an ideal fiction and cannot be the aim of analysis. The aim is rather recognition and acceptance of the constant oscillation of psychic movement between the manifestations of desire and the defenses against them. Analysis itself is an experience par excellence of this process. The analysis is a mytho-historical event and cannot become history in the strict sense. There is a historical element to analysis, but there is also the re-experiencing of the past in another specific historical moment, that of the analysis.

Some analysts feel that the personal myth should be taken apart and the repression lifted in order to reconstruct the history of the patient, while others believe that the goal is to discover the mythology of the patient, to find the symbolic value of the patient's fantasy life. Potamianou thinks that analyst and analysand should learn that there is never total control over primary process, and that secondary process is always subject to the incursions of desire.

What role can we permit personal myths to play in our psychic economy? The personal myth is the central kernel in all material the analysand brings to analysis. It consists of a representational constellation that links and unites three primary fantasies—the primal scene, seduction, and castration. The economic purpose of the personal myth is certainly that of repression, but it also constitutes the most personal mode of fashioning one's own reality, of building and maintaining the interior world unique to each individual.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

In this sometimes amusing and cynical paper Barande discusses analytic innovations from the standpoint of memory, or, more exactly, the failure to recall what has gone before. Analysts are subject to lapses of memory concerning Freud and what

176

they owe him. The analysts' memory within the analytic session is deceptive, for the speaker, as analyst, is talking about his own memory, with no control or way of validation, while subject to secondary process elaboration. It might be better to examine the analyst's memory in writings about theory. What the analyst writes can be compared with the corpus of Freudian theory as a reference point to examine the analyst's memory. He considers the writings of Roazen on Tausk, and of Masson on the supposed abandonment of the seduction theory, as examples of the way that writers now tend to calumniate Freud. There is much of this in the lay press, but that would not matter as much if it did not reappear in internal attacks within the psychoanalytic community. The appearance of the Freud correspondence is eagerly awaited for possible gossip. There are accusations against older analysts concerning the war years. For Barande, numerous contemporary efforts at theorizing suffer, just like hysterics, from disturbances of memory. Freud is forgotten; his theories are reinvented or turned against him. Masson, Viderman, Torok and N. Abraham are among the writers Barande criticizes as proponents of what he regards as fashionable modes of contemporary theorizing.

Construction. Introduction to a Question of Memory in Supervision. Pierre Fedida. Pp. 1141-1149.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

Fedida discusses modes of conceptualizing supervision. Perhaps the classical view offers an objective model of the supervised case: the material is discussed by supervisor and supervisee, with emphasis on observation, selective attention, memory, and synthesis. This medical or scientific view emphasizes the case, patient, treatment, etc., as imaginary objects for the contract of exchanges between supervisor and supervisee. In contrast is the model drawn from communications theory: the supervisor is said to serve less as a superego function and more as a facilitator of communication between the supervisor, the treating analyst, and the progress of the treatment. This communicational aspect is contrasted with the emphasis on memory in psychoanalytic work. Fedida proposes that the use of the communications model increases interest in psychic functioning and co-functioning in their interrelation, and moves away from the anecdotal method of the supervisee recounting all that can be remembered of a session. There is a third way of viewing the supervisor/supervisee session, that is, of someone who is speaking before an analyst. The last view gets away from supposing there are two types of analytic work—treatment and supervision—in favor, simply, of what is said before an analyst. Such a view, with no separate theory of supervision, emphasizes the unity of psychoanalysis.

Who Killed Virginia Woolf? a Psychobiography

By Alma Halbert Bond, Ph.D. New York: Human Sciences Press, Inc., 1989. 200 pp.

Theodore Jacobs

Theodore Jacobs

Theodore J. Jacobs
NEW YORK

Theodore Jacobs  

If psychoanalysis is rightly called the impossible profession, the writing of the psychobiography of a deceased artist must surely be the least possible of the impossible tasks a psychoanalyst can undertake. Not only is one working in the field of applied analysis, terrain hazardous to the health of the naïve and unwary, but one has set oneself the awesome task of plumbing the deepest motivations of a creative individual whom one can know only through her or his works and the works of others.

This is the challenge that Alma Bond, a practicing psychoanalyst, has accepted in writing Who Killed Virginia Woolf?, a study of the multiple and complex factors that contributed to Virginia Woolf's decision in 1941 to commit suicide by drowning.

Bond's approach to this investigation, surprising for one who, as a psychoanalyst, must avoid taking judgmental positions, is more like that of a prosecuting attorney than that of an objective scientist. The title of her book, with its clear implication of murder and its reference to Edward Albee's play, Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?

DISCUSSION: Dr. Leonard Shengold said that the presentation had given the audience a penetrating view of how Dr. Weinshel works and thinks. The case was not spectacular, as it included flaws and limitations of the analyst. It represented the best in the self-observation of an analyst, permitting him to function as "the conscience of the analysis." Dr. Shengold noted that the patient had been a victim of parental "soul murder." As a child she had been "brainwashed" by both her parents: emotionally deprived and psychologically rejected by her mother, she was led to doubt her perceptions of her mother's crazy behavior by both parents. She protected herself from awareness of her rage by repression and masochistic defenses, accompanied by an idealization of her mother, her father, and her analysts. Another issue involved was Dr. Weinshel's burden in being of "good character." He wanted to do and give too much to his patient. This was his positive countertransference, and to the abused child as an adult patient, this presented a danger of traumatic repetition. It opened the patient up to the horrors of overstimulation, rejection, humiliation, and finally rage and terror. In response to his countertransference the patient defended herself with isolation and dampening of love and rage. She wished for love from the analyst, yet guarded herself against the danger inherent in it. Dr. Shengold believed that only the revival of this dangerous love and hate within the transference could lead to change. The patient had to learn to tolerate loving the analyst in order to come to terms with her rage. The analyst's interpretations had to "evoke emotions that can release the patient's ability to love." Did Dr. Weinshel's good character help or hinder this process? Dr. Shengold was not sure there is a definite answer, but he believed it helps when good character is "tempered and thereby made more acceptable by honesty, toughness, and the ability to see, and to help the patient see, how that goodness can be used in the service of transference and countertransference resistances." Dr. Weinshel's self-observation and awareness of two people in a psychoanalytic process became "an insight-provoking enablement that allowed for diminishment of the terror, rage and longing, and for reduction of the need for idealization and denial.

The Human Core. The Intrapsychic Base of Behavior. Vol. I: Action Within the Structural View; Vol. II: from Anxiety to Integrity

By Leo Rangell, M.D. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, Inc., 1990. 959 pp.

Arnold Richards

Arnold Richards

Arnold D. Richards
NEW YORK

Arnold Richards  

Like Arlow and Brenner, who have effected major revisions in Freudian theory, Leo Rangell extends psychoanalytic theory into new areas. His contributions, like theirs, are not patchwork jobs for an ailing theory but rather proposed solutions to important psychoanalytic problems. In the present collection, 35 papers are selected from the more than 300 Rangell has written over the course of four decades.

In Volume I, Action within the Structural View, Rangell re-examines the problem of anxiety in psychoanalytic theory and considers problems of choice, responsibility, and integrity. He provides a set of concepts and constructs dealing with aspects of human behavior that very few psychoanalytic theorists have even considered. As in all his works, his solutions to problems are grounded firmly in the work of Freud and his successors, chief among them Heinz Hartmann, Otto Fenichel, and David Rapaport. Rangell argues that his "postulation of unconscious choice conflict and the contiguous concept of unconscious ego decision-making… is … quite different from the conventional type of oppositional conflict which leads to a solution by compromise formation" (p. 14). To Freud's concept of signal anxiety and of thought as experimental action he appends four additional concepts: "intrapsychic process" as against intersystemic conflict between, for example, ego and id; a new ego function referred to as unconscious decision-making; the syndrome of the compromise of integrity; and the exercise of will as an aspect of ego autonomy.

In "Psychoanalysis, Affects, and the 'Human Core,'" written in 1964, Rangell introduces his concept of "the human core," which is marked by "the unconscious rather than conscious, the intrapsychic rather than internal-external, and the conflictful rather than the conflict-free and autonomous …" (p. 61). This harks back to Ernst Kris's definition of psychoanalysis as human behavior seen from the point of view of unconscious conflict.

Six Steps in the Treatment of Borderline Personality Organization

By Vamik D. Volkan, M.D. Northvale, NJ/London: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1987. 232 pp.

Michael Porder

Michael Porder

Michael S. Porder
NEW YORK

Michael Porder  

This book is a thoughtful, lucid contribution to the analytic literature on the psychological development and treatment of borderline patients. Volkan is a gifted analyst, and his contributions are a significant addition to the long list of analytic practitioners who work with very disturbed patients. Furthermore, he is an engaging writer who makes his points clearly and punctuates them with engrossing clinical examples. I heartily recommend this book to all analysts and therapists who work with severely disturbed patients.

The book centers around two axes. The first encompasses Volkan's observations on the developmental conflicts and the fixation points of nine psychosis-prone patients and his sequential treatment plan for good analytic results with these patients. The second is a detailed case history of the fascinating treatment of one such severely disturbed young woman. Unfortunately, I do not believe that Volkan's generalizations represent an easy recipe for most therapists to follow, because he has unique gifts of timing and interpretation, as well as an exceptional ability to regress along with his patients that may not be available to many practitioners. As with so many other treatment recommendations for the successful approach to disturbed patients, technique becomes, in large part, an extension of one's character. As Volkan himself indicates, if one is unfamiliar with treating such patients, then it is necessary to have supervision with an experienced therapist before proceeding.

Volkan's ideas are firmly rooted in object relations theory. He believes that the conflicts in his patients are the result of "splitting" mechanisms, as described by Kernberg. He agrees with Buie that the development of ambivalence, accompanied by pain and discomfort, is an essential step in the treatment of these patients. He contrasts these conflicts with those centering around guilt and repression that are seen in neurotic patients. However, he does agree with Abend and co-workers that all kinds of defense mechanisms are observed in these patients and that oedipal, libidinal, and aggressive conflicts are always present, although heavily influenced by preoedipal conflicts.

[[RunningHead]]

The Work of Culture. Symbolic Transformation in Psychoanalysis and Anthropology

By Gananath Obeyesekere. Chicago/London: The University of Chicago Press, 1990. 354 pp.

Werner Muensterberger

Werner Muensterberger

Werner Muensterberger
NEW YORK

Werner Muensterberger  

"The aim of anthropology is the enlargement of the human discourse," Clifford Geertz persuasively observed.1 This is what Obeyesekere's 1982 Lewis Henry Morgan Lectures achieve. In this volume they are considerably expanded (289 pages, plus extensive footnotes and bibliography) and presented as four lectures whose headings succinctly outline the dimensions of the author's concepts and approach. He combines vivid ethnographic field accounts with South Asian mythologies. The focus is on the manifest variations of oedipal currents. He paints a lively picture of them against the background of the prevailing ethos ("Buddhist Sri Lanka glorifies the son who kills the father, whereas Hindu India glorifies the son who submits" [p. 138]) and characteristic life styles. The study culminates in a broad and involved exposition that occasionally is not easy to follow. He supports Freud's early topographic model in his effort to gain understanding of some of the origins and vicissitudes of human interaction.

It is not often that one has the privilege of reviewing a work of rare erudition. It deals with the essential affinity of basic human predicaments and the modalities of object relationships. Obeyesekere integrates detailed field observations made in his home country of Sri Lanka with what he gained from many years of Western education, not only in his own field but also in twentieth century sociology and philosophy.

1Geertz, C. (1973): The Interpretation of Cultures. New York: Basic Books, p. 14.299

Psychoanalytic Inquiry. X, 1990

Psychotherapy as a Trial for Psychoanalysis. Leonard Horwitz. Pp. 43-65.

James Edgar

James Edgar

James Edgar  

The conversion to psychoanalysis from psychotherapy with the same analyst is a recent phenomenon. In 1976 only 12% of analytic cases had first been in psychotherapy with their analyst; 40% had had psychotherapy with a different analyst. Horwitz discusses the desirability of psychotherapy as a trial for analysis, rather than a trial analysis in those cases where there is serious doubt about a patient's analyzability. He points out that although a trial analysis was recommended by Freud, psychoanalytic psychotherapy as we now know it was not then available. He suggests that a failed "trial analysis" may be unnecessarily traumatic for these questionable cases. Some recent literature regarding the distinction between psychotherapy and psychoanalysis, examples of converting from therapy to analysis, and therapy as preparatory for analysis is reviewed. Contemporary Psychoanalysis. XXVIII, 1992

Discussion. Jay R. Greenberg. Pp. 277-285.

J. Leblanc

J. Leblanc

J. Leblanc  

Greenberg prefaces his discussion with comments on some recent "attacks" on the validity of psychoanalytic propositions (Grünbaum, Daniel Stern). He suggests that some analysts seek a measure of safety in associating with an "adjacent" discipline rather than bearing the intractable ambiguity of our clinical work.

On this score, Greenberg lauds the exquisite sensitivity of the above presenters, Sandler and Pine, to the vulnerabilities of their patients. He underscores their concerns about people who may be disorganized by the interpretive process and be unable to maintain self-cohesion. But he suggests there may be a "developmental morality" here (Kohut). Developmentalists, under the guise of the "holding environment," or "ego defect," may fail to negotiate with their patients the textured transactions of needs and wishes in the analytic setting, i.e., with appropriate abstinence. Greenberg emphasizes, "We don't tend to think why some people need abstinence." We rationalize our departures as due to developmental needs.

Contemporary Psychoanalysis. XXVIII, 1992

Discussion. Robert B. Shapiro. Pp. 286-294.

J. Leblanc

J. Leblanc

J. Leblanc  

Shapiro views the developmental perspective as the overriding organizer for the individual seen in analysis. While shifting focus in analysis, the analyst utilizes the developmental perspective as a major backdrop which permits the integration of immediate experience. Shapiro proposes that the presence of this backdrop helps the therapist maintain his equilibrium in the midst of countertransference feelings. Knowing the patient's life and its evolution permits the analyst to endure the disruptive emotions which inevitably arise. It brings about an emotional detachment that paradoxically allows the analyst to engage the patient more empathically.

Shapiro questions Sandler's technical description of the developmental layering of resistances. He proposes that the analytic process is generally more fluent, less "neat or linear." He also suggests that Sandler may minimize the primary influence of early relationships. Transference countertransference re-enactments suggest early historical formulations of the data—which require further validation. Finally, Shapiro agrees with Pine that it is useful to offer patients a way to understand their early life stories.

Portal Aspects of Memory Overlay in Psychoanalysis: An Object Relations Contribution to Screen Memory Phenomena. Moshe Halevi Spero. Pp. 79-103.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Spero offers a thorough discussion of the contributions of many writers to understanding the nature and formation of screen memories, a discussion that cannot be usefully summarized in a brief abstract. Spero supports the use of a new term, portal detail, to designate a variant of the screen memory in which "distorted details" of an early memory recalled in analysis lead to a later memory which contains "record of the attempted emergence into consciousness of the source [early] memory in its full traumatic force." Such a portal detail has a screening function; it may be a symbol or a part-object. All this is greatly clarified by two striking case examples.

The Role of Fantasy in the Treatment of a Severely Disturbed Child. Adele M. Kaufman. Pp. 235-256.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Case presentations of children who engage in fully expressed fantasies have great value both in providing evidence to support or refute theory and in illustrating a therapist's ways of working. Kaufman's patient richly elaborated five basic fantasies. She persuasively describes the child's offerings and the therapist's responses to them. Such matters as fears of abandonment, identification with the aggressor, regressions caused by fears—for example, when Kaufman moved her office—and many other processes are vividly shown. This is a noteworthy paper, highly instructive. The child improved in treatment, and Kaufman convincingly discusses the reasons for her improvement.

The writer explores the reasons for, and uses of, a woman's fantasy that she had an ideal older brother. The meanings of the fantasy were numerous and complex. It expressed identifications and defenses, and was clearly related to her later relations with a man. The fantasy contributed in a basic way to her character.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Yorke and his colleagues, some of whom treated patients referred to in the paper, offer a thorough review of shame: its distinction from guilt, its sources, and its defensive value. There is an interesting discussion of various characteristics of shame, its relation to other feelings, and its relation to superego and sense of self. Much

343

attention is paid to how shame develops, its relation to developmental phases, to the insides and outsides of the body, to sphincter control. Shamelessness is considered. Besides its presentation of some thoroughly developed ideas, the paper seems likely to stimulate new investigations into aspects of shame.

Some Issues Affecting Termination: The Treatment of a High-Risk Adolescent. Marianne Parsons. Pp. 437-458.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Parsons presents clearly and with necessary detail the analysis, still incomplete, of a girl long known to the Anna Freud Center, who had undergone two partial analyses; she was fifteen when she began with Parsons. The bulk of the paper is a discussion of many problems about termination. Peggy had suffered parental deprivation: her father mostly absent, her mother neurotic, selfish, and inadequate, yet trying to do her best for her child. This history greatly complicated termination of treatment: Peggy could not easily work out her oedipal conflict; she faced realistic anxieties; her mourning, which is required in termination, was interfered with. Her mother could not let her go, and the patient was affected by the loss of two previous therapists. Parsons lucidly shows how these and other difficulties impeded—and will impede, for the analysis is by no means complete—Peggy's termination.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Schmukler offers a fine account of the six-year-long analysis of a boy, starting when he was ten. At first he had obsessive-compulsive symptoms and made great progress in dropping them and becoming mature, ready to become an adult. Her discussion of the case is brief. One might have been glad of more, but both patient and therapist were so articulate that what is going on is quite clear, a virtue not always found in case presentations. This case teaches us important facts about obsessional behavior as well as about the ambivalence, anxieties, and progressions in transference found in termination with an adolescent.

The Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XLV, 1990

Who's Afraid in Virginia Woolf? Clues to Early Sexual Abuse in Literature. Lenore C. Terr. Pp. 533-546.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

In spite of its unfortunate title, this is an important study of Woolf's life and works. It shows how the early sexual abuse by her half-brothers determined her character; and how the characters she writes about show the same traits as Woolf herself. Terr believes that Woolf suffered from a "type II trauma-stress disorder." Persons with this trouble tend to be, among other things, "emotionally numbed," to use "splitting," dissociations, and turning against the self. Woolf was much like that: she was, for example, sexually anesthetic, or nearly so, and so are the people in her books. Terr has much more of interest to say about Woolf and her novels.

A striking point Terr makes is her own response to Woolf's writings. At least some of them leave her unmoved. She suggests that this is so because we never get close to what it feels like to a child to be abused sexually, and in many parts of Woolf's writings we remain equally remote from events—unclear as to what they are and how the subjects respond to them.

345

A Response to Critics. Fred Weinstein. Pp. 61-69.

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin  

Weinstein responds to several articles in this issue criticizing his book History and Theory After the Fall. Of particular interest to psychoanalytic readers is his response to Richard L. Schoenwald's essay, "Getting On With It," regarding the evolution of psychoanalysis over the years. Weinstein cites Robert Wallerstein and Joseph Sandler, agreeing that there is no warrant for any assertion in psychoanalysis beyond assertions about the clinical data of the consulting room. Psychoanalysis has ended up in a proliferation of points of view, according to Weinstein, because of the flight into theory that departs from closeness to clinical experience.

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin  

In an issue devoted to discussion of the work of Robert J. Lifton, Strozier and Flynn comment that although Lifton has continually emphasized his debt to psychoanalytic theory, and especially to his mentor, Erik Erikson, he has in fact moved toward a different model. Lifton's discussion of the quest for "symbolic immortality" distinguishes itself from Freud's notion of the self's continual denial of death, positing a middle knowledge or partial awareness of death accompanied by nonpathological forms of denial.

The Psychohistory Review: Studies of Motivation in History and Culture. XX, 1991/92

The Rise and Fall of Bruno Bettelheim. Paul Roazen. Pp. 221-250.

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin  

Roazen examines the role of Bruno Bettelheim in the history of psychoanalysis, emphasizing his famous study of Nazi concentration camps. Examining the reaction of other prisoners, such as their defense of identifying with the aggressor, Roazen reviews Bettelheim's famous discussion of self-defeating responses to aggression and how he upheld the ideal of the individual as an autonomous and self-reliant entity. Roazen writes about the importance of Bettelheim in his own education in such areas as autism, and the implications of the unconscious for social philosophy. He also assesses Bettelheim's contribution to psychohistory in reference to other great figures, such as Erich Fromm, Erik Erikson, and Hannah Arendt. Roazen notes Bettleheim's movement—in such books as Symbolic Wounds, Dialogues with Mothers, and in his critique of the Ernest Jones biography of Freud—into original unorthodox positions. At first Roazen seems to have found Bettelheim's arguments persuasive, particularly as intellectual autobiography, and as an integration of what he had learned from the concentration camps and from Freud; yet he traces his own growing disillusionment with Bettelheim's egotistical obsession with autonomy. Finally, Roazen considers the implications of Bettelheim's suicide upon his work, as well as the troubling phenomenon of how many psychoanalysts have ended their lives by suicide.

[[RunningHead]]

The Psychohistory Review: Studies of Motivation in History and Culture. XX, 1991/92

Adolf Hitler: The Evil Self. Hyman Muslin. Pp. 251-270.

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin  

Taking the approach of psychoanalytic self psychology, Muslin seeks to understand Adolf Hitler and the group-self responses of the German people to him during the rise and fall of the Nazi reign, through Hitler's tenure as chancellor, and during the military phase of the Third Reich. Muslin describes Hitler's self as enfeebled and unformed, depleted of values and self-regard, with an exceedingly diminished capacity for accepting nurturance and direction. The self psychological analysis understands much of Hitler's behavior in terms of this inadequacy, involving compensatory tactics of aloofness and grandiosity, narcissistic deficiency states, and vicious attacks on seeming persecutors. In the absence of object relationships and consequent lack of self-equilibrium, Hitler strove to achieve national equilibrium for Germany by displacing onto others a selfobject transference psychotic reaction from the paternal selfobject of his childhood. Hitler's distintegration anxiety, arising from self-fragmentation, required increasingly vast compensatory measures. Unable to show neediness or defect, fearful of exposing any deficiency or corresponding dependency, he externalized this fear into retaliating against imagined punishers by such grandiose measures as mass killings. All of this took place within a selfobject/self-dyad between Hitler and the German people.

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Society of New England, East

October 28, 1991. PSYCHOANALYSIS IN CZECHOSLOVAKIA. Michael Sebek, Ph.D.

In the first of three precirculated papers, Dr. Sebek, the President of the Czechoslovakia Psychoanalytic Institute, discussed the history of the psychoanalytic movement in Czechoslovakia. Beginning in 1920, two groups co-existed, one in Prague around Dr. N. Ossipow from Russia and the other in eastern Slovakia guided by the Czech psychiatrist, Dr. Jar Stuchlík. In 1931 Emanuel Windholz, influenced by Stuchlík and trained in Berlin, began his psychoanalytic practice in Prague. In 1926 the Czech Study Group for Psychoanalysis was recognized by the IPA at the Marienbad Congress. O. Fenichel, A. Reich, and S. Bornstein lived in Prague in the 1930's and were active in the psychoanalytic training and education of the Czech Study Group until the beginning of the war. The Study Group ended with Hitler's occupation of Czechoslovakia. Some of its members emigrated, mostly to the United States; others perished in concentration camps. The only remaining survivor, Theodor Dosuzkov, trained by Fenichel and Reich, continued the psychoanalytic tradition during the war and re-established the Czech Study Group in 1946. Following the communist putsch, the group continued to function underground.

Dr. Sebek spoke of the vicissitudes of psychoanalysis under Stalinism. Pavlov's reflexology replaced psychoanalysis in the official journal. This period ended abruptly in 1958, and it was not until 1962 that some liberalization in Czechoslovakian society began, at which time some of Freud's works were published, as well as articles by several local analysts. Psychoanalysts continued to work underground, in spite of the edict against private practice. They were also employed in psychiatric clinics as psychologists and psychiatrists. Medical professionals knew about them while not officially acknowledging them. Dr. Sebek described in some detail the lives and work of three psychoanalysts under the Stalinist rule: Theodor Dosuzkov, who wrote and published nearly two hundred works in several languages; Ladislav Haas, who emigrated to London in 1964 and became a member of the British Psycho-Analytical Society; and Otokar Kucera, who trained several members of the current generation of Czech psychoanalysts.

[[RunningHead]]

Jacques Lacan & Co. a History of Psychoanalysis in France, 1925-1985

By Elisabeth Roudinesco. Translated by Jeffrey Mehlman. Chicago: The University of Chicago Press, 1990. 766 pp.

Mitchell Wilson

Mitchell Wilson

Mitchell Wilson
BERKELEY, CA

Mitchell Wilson  

Elisabeth Roudinesco begins her monumental history of psychoanalysis in France with a moving, darkly rendered account of André Breton rising to the defense of his friend, Max Ernst. Thirty pages later we read of Breton's profound disappointment when he met Freud, who seemed to him old and ordinary. From these novelistic scenes we are given to understand that the encounter between what Roudinesco calls "the message from Vienna" and its French audience will be passionate and difficult. She unfurls a vast Western landscape upon which cultural and intellectual traditions collide. Armed with deeply held beliefs about the nature of psychoanalysis, individuals march across countries and continents to fight for their Freudian cause. Lives assume epic proportions. Psychoanalytic institutions rise and fall as the dismantling of them becomes an essential part of the French psychoanalytic ethos. This English edition is Volume Two of her original French work, which she calls The Hundred Years' Battle. As described by Roudinesco, the stakes of battle are high: institutional power through doctrinal influence. What is the authentic nature of psychoanalysis? This is the central question over which these different doctrinal tendencies repeatedly battle.

Roudinesco describes the development of ideas with such skill that they become nearly personified (we end up caring about the life or death of an idea). We read in detail about the Surrealist movement, its particular appropriation of psychoanalysis, and its influence on the second generation of French analysts. We read about the intricate relationships between the early years of Bolshevism, Marxism, Pavlovian psychology, and Wilhelm Reich. We learn about Catholicism, Maoism, Hegel, structural linguistics, deconstruction—all in relation to the development of psychoanalysis in France after World War II. There are forays into the movies of Hitchcock, Wilder, and Chaplin.

La Maternité Et Le Féminin. (Maternity and the Feminine.)

By Danièle Brun. Paris: Éditions Denoël, 1990. 280 pp.

Richard Waugaman

Richard Waugaman

Richard M. Waugaman
ROCKVILLE, MD

Richard Waugaman  

Most of this book's thirteen chapters previously appeared as articles in a variety of French journals; two more papers constitute appendices. The scope of the book is femininity broadly defined, encompassing a variety of problems in both female as well as male psychology. Brun writes with originality, aptly melding clinical and theoretical interests. She skillfully examines clinical observations in microscopic detail, then places them in the context of the theoretical contributions she develops. Ever respectful of the ambiguities of the analytic situation, she exemplifies the great attention to nuances of language, as well as the close reading of Freud, that characterize contemporary French psychoanalysis.

In her preface, Brun cites two sources for the papers in this book: first, her work on unconscious processes in parents whose children have been cured of cancer; second, material from her analytic practice that illuminates issues concerning femininity. She links these two sources of data by emulating Freud and studying unique instances of pathology (such as having a child cured of cancer) for what they tell us about more typical analytic material.

Adult Analysis and Childhood Sexual Abuse

Edited by Howard B. Levine. Hillsdale, NJ/London: The Analytic Press, 1990. 231 pp.

Austin Silber

Austin Silber

Austin Silber
NEW YORK

Austin Silber  

The scope of this book is clinical. "Its aim is to explore the problems of technique that are often encountered in attempts to treat in psychoanalysis [those] adults who were sexually abused as children" (p. 4). It is divided into three main sections: Introduction and Overview, Clinical Considerations and Psychoanalytic Process, and Issues of Technique. The introduction reviews the history of the importance of actual trauma in Freud's early view of neurosogenesis. It covers ground which is currently the object of renewed analytic interest.

The complicated questions addressed by the contributors are made explicit by the questions Levine poses in the introduction: "We are unable to accurately evaluate the nature and basis for Freud's evidence in formulating the seduction theory. Thus, the possibility exists that the still nascent stage of the analytic theory and technique on which he had to depend left Freud with a methodology that was not adequate to the task of discerning actual from fantasied childhood traumata and that he was led to his conclusions in part by his theoretical preconceptions of what he would find, rather than the data of his clinical encounters" (p. 18).

Leon Balter

Leon Balter

Leon Balter
NEW YORK

Leon Balter  

This volume contains an extremely varied array of essays which in one way or another justify its title. Taking into account their subject matter, their theoretical orientations (psychoanalytic or otherwise), and the disciplines represented, that is about where their commonality ends. However, there does seem to be a shared agenda for the volume as a whole: to save religion from "classical," or "traditional," psychoanalysis—the latter perceived as critical, even inimical, to religion. The editors are explicit on this point. For they refer to most of the "articles [as] all bound together in ecumenical resistance to Freudian reductionistic interpretation of all religion" (p. xv). This pervasive animosity toward classical psychoanalysis makes little distinction between the person of "Godless" Sigmund Freud, the current practicing classical psychoanalyst, and the theory of classical psychoanalysis.

This attitude is dramatically exemplified by Joseph H. Smith, one of the two editors.

Paul W. Pruyser, who died in 1987, was an esteemed clinical psychologist at the Menninger Clinic whose writings on psychology and religion have been widely read. He was born in Holland, where he took part in the resistance against the German occupation during the Second World War, but lived in the United States most of his life. The papers included in this book have all appeared in print before. They are gathered here, as the editors write, to bring them together "as seminal anchor points for understanding his approach.

Treating Suicidelike Behavior in a Preschooler

By Paul V. Trad, M.D. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, 1990. 476 pp.

Edward Tobe

Edward Tobe

Edward H. Tobe
MARLTON, NJ

Edward Tobe  

Trad presents a case history of Alex, who was three years four months of age when he entered into a three-year-long treatment. Alex was referred by his school because of aggressive outbursts, self-destructive thoughts, and withdrawn states. He expressed fantasies about using a knife to cut his belly. There were fantasies about running to a window and perhaps jumping out of the window. Trad describes Alex's family as very disturbed, manifesting problems with anger and depression. The author does not make clear the exact format of the treatment. Apparently, Trad treated Alex individually two or three times a week and also met with "the family." The author refers to his treatment as not psychoanalytic but eclectic. I had the impression that the treatment at times involved meeting with and perhaps treating the mother individually, at times meeting with the mother and father together, and at times meeting with the mother and Alex together. The case is presented strictly from a psychological standpoint.

The author starts with Alex's life history. He gives a picture of a very dysfunctional family. Both parents struggled with powerful angry feelings. As an example, after father left the family home, he returned to burn the family photographs. Mother and Alex came home to find the ashes. The description of the treatment process is quite interesting. At times, Trad offers very detailed material from sessions with Alex. Courageously, Trad even presents one of his own dreams, which occurred during his treatment of Alex. In the dream, Trad awakens in bed and realizes that Alex is in great danger. On a rainy night Trad races to Alex's home after failing to reach Alex by phone. When he arrives, Trad discovers mother's very seductive behavior. Trad sees Alex hiding while mother denies Alex's presence, but alludes to the presence of a male lover. He offers ideas on how this dream helped him better understand Alex. In this early section of the book, the author offers suggestions about Alex's psychodynamics. Alex did appear to benefit from the treatment.

Lee Grossman

Lee Grossman

Lee Grossman  

Finkelstein contends that the complexity of the superego has been underappreciated, particularly its role in moral responsibility and in an individual's conflicting value systems. Analysts are more likely to notice the harsh superego than the superego problems in the patient who defensively avoids appropriate guilt for his or her actions. It may be difficult to question immoral behavior in a way the patient can accept. The analytic situation itself may obscure such issues by overemphasizing the superego's prohibitions (e.g., against free association) and by the patient's efforts to "behave" for the analyst. Finkelstein agrees with the position of Wallace, who holds that the individual is morally responsible for his or her actions, regardless of whether they are driven or freely chosen. He surveys some modern thinkers on superego development, particularly Gilligan on gender differences and Hoffman on socialization. He suggests that analysts must expand their understanding of the complexity of the superego concept and must address moral issues in treatment, albeit without moralizing.

The author approaches the Dora case and especially Dora's first dream in analysis from the point of view of anthropology and attempts to integrate this view with earlier psychological and linguistic interpretations. By claiming that the Dora case contains elements of the incest taboo, the exchange of women, and rules of kinship and marriage, Banks challenges the premise that the distance between psychological and cultural realms cannot be bridged. The theme of the relation between sexual taboos and the exchange of women is detailed in the work on kinship of Lévi-Strauss, who states that women are the most precious gifts exchanged between families and groups when a marriage takes place.

On the Phylogeny of the Oedipus Complex: Psychoanalytic Aspects of the Ethology of Anthropoid Apes. Reijo Holmström. Pp. 271-316.

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar  

This paper seeks to examine the evolutionary origins of the oedipus complex through an ethological approach. The author hopes that we can construct a model of our own primordial background by comparing ourselves with contemporary animal species. The animals chosen for this are the anthropoid apes, more specifically, the chimpanzee and the gorilla, animals extensively studied by the ethologists Good-all and Fossey. The paper focuses on a constellation in these species viewed as similar to aspects of the oedipus complex and involving the development of the males. Its aim is to show that the oedipal constellation has undergone a gradual evolutionary development and is universal in anthropoid ape communities. The author gives a number of examples of what he sees as this oedipal constellation, including a description, in chimpanzees, of the way male and female infants try very hard to interfere with the mating of mature males and females. This behavior is tolerated until the infant is four or five at which time the young male will be threatened or worse if he tries to disrupt the mating. In both these species mother-son mating is inhibited to the point of being almost nonexistent. The author discusses developmental considerations in the anthropoid apes. For instance, in chimpanzees there is a long period of dependence on the mother resulting in great loyalty, along with an early sexual interest in females in estrus. However, even during estrus the mother is treated by her son as a mother and not as a female in heat. Holmström stresses his belief that the son's early and prolonged dependence on the mother produces a bond so strong it precludes sexual activity. From the evolutionary perspective, the selective advantage of this incest taboo is that it prevents excessive inbreeding and strengthens the defensive capabilities of the group and the safety of the offspring. A central hypothesis of the paper is that the oedipus constellation, in which the author includes the incest taboo, is a basic force in the development of anthropoid apes and human beings, and constitutes a fundamental evolutionary advantage. He believes that the oedipus constellation stimulates warfare between groups and that warfare itself provides tremendous selective pressure on a species, perhaps the principal evolutionary pressure. The advent of the two-parent family in humans is discussed, along with positive and negative implications of the oedipus complex and how it effects the survival of both the species and the world.

Sybil Ginsburg  

In a 1926 B'nai B'rith address, Freud discussed his Jewishness by referring to "obscure emotional forces," "a clear consciousness of inner identity," and "a common mental construction." Fin de siècle Vienna was rife with anti-Semitism. Jews were considered a fixed biological race; and such adjectives as prosaic, unknowable, anxious, hysterical, and smelly were used in descriptions of the common characteristics of this "race." Part of the thesis of this paper is that Freud and his followers had internalized, and were in conflict over, these anti-Semitic attitudes. Freud certainly expressed a mixture of pride and prejudice toward his Jewishness in numerous communications. Also, although he insisted that the science of psychoanalysis was independent of race, he remained concerned that it might be impeded by a strong Jewish "spirit." He hoped that "Aryan" followers, such as Jung, would help "free" psychoanalysis. Gilman proceeds to Freud's definition of gender.

Rodman Gilder—1918-1993

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Rodman Gilder was for twenty-seven years an important participant in the editing of The Psychoanalytic Quarterly: active in the selection of papers for publication and the checking and revision of them. He contributed to our annual meetings, and among these other services we like to recall his arranging, with Mary Crowther, and later with Jo Shapiro, our delightful Christmas parties at the Century Association.

First, the facts of his professional life. Born in New York, he attended school there and at the innovative Fountain Valley School in Colorado. After Harvard, he was graduated from the Columbia College of Physicians and Surgeons and received his psychoanalytic training—certified in psychoanalysis of both adults and children—at Columbia's Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research, as well as at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute. For most of his life he taught at Columbia, and in recent years at the New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center, Westchester Division, and he practiced analysis and psychotherapy at his home in Scarsdale. In the Second World War he served in the Navy. He was a President of the Westchester Psychoanalytic Society, and did much work for public agencies in the county.

It is especially noteworthy that he organized and led a continuing group meeting for the parents of children with cancer. This he did for many years, though he found it emotionally exhausting; the outlook for such children was especially grim in those days.

In his introduction to this extremely worthwhile and surprisingly comprehensive textbook on psychodynamic psychiatry, Glen Gabbard comments on his reasons for writing the book. He tells of speaking to residents, psychiatrists, and other mental health professionals around the country who repeatedly expressed concern about their inadequate training in psychodynamic psychiatry. He also relates his own disquiet regarding the "unnecessary polarization between biological and psychodynamic approaches within psychiatry" (p. xiv). This book is Gabbard's extremely ambitious effort to answer the needs of psychiatric residents and clinical psychiatrists for an up-to-date, relatively comprehensive textbook that correlates dynamic understanding and therapies, including individual psychotherapy, group psychotherapy, family/marital therapy, dynamic pharmacotherapy, and dynamically informed hospital treatment, with the major DSM-III-R diagnoses, thus meeting a need which many professionals experience when confronted with the essentially descriptive nature of DSM-III-R.

This task is a tall order, particularly when one considers that Gabbard's goal is to produce a one-volume text "that does not require a forklift to transport it" (p. xiv).

Wayne Myers

Wayne Myers

Wayne A. Myers
NEW YORK

Wayne Myers  

This volume contains a number of poignant essays by a sage group of older psychoanalysts. The first of these, "On Growing Old," was

639

written by the late Samuel Atkin and his son, Adam. It is largely concerned with the elder Atkin's struggles with physical illness. He notes with pleasure the modifications in his ego structure which he attained while adapting to his limitations. He further speaks of his capacity to learn new skills, while commenting on the rigidity in his perception of his body image despite the deterioration of his physical state. Another observation, echoed by many of the contributors to this volume, and one with which I heartily concur, is that ego development continues throughout the life cycle and does not stop with the closure of adolescence. Atkin further suggests that reminiscing about the past is a way of mourning for one's lost self. The accompanying piece, "Elegy for a Widow," by Edith Atkin, details her struggles with depressive affect after her husband's death. It is a model for understanding the variety of losses an individual undergoes when a lifelong mate is lost.

Bernard Bandler's "The Aging Process" also emphasizes the idea of emotional growth in later life. He sees the issue of retirement, so often mandated in various fields at a specific age (say 65), as a "dress rehearsal for death." He describes how a brush with death mobilized in him a flood of vivid childhood memories and existentially intensified his desire to complete a work on female writers he was immersed in.

In "Perspective at Seventy-Seven of Prejudice, Conflict, and Aloneness," Siegfried Berthelsdorf speaks of retirement as a graduation into the elder age category and of the importance of the function of reminiscence for the aged. Virginia Clower, in "Aging in a Mirror," notes that her close contact with aging relatives in her youth gave her a tolerance for "progressive decrepitude." She observes that early development in the individual is incremental, whereas postmaturational change is more aptly described as decremental. This decremental change feels "wrong" to the individual. It indicates to him/her an impairment in integral aspects of the self. Clower sees the fear of dying as a less immediate threat to the older person than the fear of helplessness and loss of autonomy. And, finally, she notes that the normally aging person must reintegrate in the course of decremental loss in order to retain a sense of identity and self-respect. I heartily concur with these extraordinarily cogent observations.

By Dorothy Judd. London: Free Association Books, 1989. 217 pp.

Moisy Shopper

Moisy Shopper

Moisy Shopper
ST. LOUIS, MO

Moisy Shopper  

Dorothy Judd, trained as a psychotherapist at Tavistock Clinic, worked with physically ill children whose life-threatening illnesses involved high-tech diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. The

658

book presents the clinical course and discusses the clinical, theoretical, and ethical issues surrounding the dying child.

The medical staff typically develops a protective distance and defensive posture toward dying children, leaving them and their parents emotionally unsupported and overwhelmed to the point of traumatization. Child therapists must assure high-quality emotional care, accompanying and at times counteracting the trauma of physical care. Judd immerses herself in the uncertainties of cancer therapy, confronting the moral and ethical questions of using hightech medical skills to prolong a life of pain, procedures, and debility despite negligible chances for survival. Her focus is that of the child's: the gradual realization of his or her fate, his or her own death.

Judd reminds us that the death of a young child is "an outrage against the natural order of things." Broadly reviewing our denying attitudes and taboos about death, Judd confronts the issues, using a Kleinian view of these phenomena: the death instinct, good and bad objects, persecutory anxieties, and the depressive position. Whether through manic defenses or idealization and transcendence, death is denied when one cannot tolerate the pain of loss. Judd confronts the theoretical/developmental paradox. Clinically, the preschool child sees death as temporary and reversible. The Kleinian preschool child uses the death instinct to develop death fantasies wherein the child then "feels that he has really destroyed the object …" (p. 24) and consequently fears retaliation from the object. Judd selected one hospitalized dying child, Bobby, to work with in psychotherapy, believing that answers and understanding will be found only through a psychodynamic approach rather than through direct interviews, questionnaires, and research protocols. A dynamic approach, she feels, recognizes the importance and pervasiveness of those defenses and fantasies which enable us to cope with death, yet paradoxically prevent us from coping with death.

Martin Silverman  

This is a book about oral longing and oral rage. The author, out of his experiences in a long career as a psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, has come to the conclusion that oral ambivalence plays a far greater role in human psychology than is generally recognized. Children start out in life, Eisenbud maintains, dominated by the illusion of an ever-present, ever-flowing, bountiful breast. The child's mother is expected to be there whenever she is wanted, lovingly ready to devote herself to meeting the child's every need.

The realization that this is only an illusion, that this ideal and idealizing expectation is not realistic and is destined to go unmet, has fateful consequences. It is inevitable that there will be frustrations, disappointments, and failure to shatter the primordial, self-serving oral fantasy of maternal perfection.

Adolescence and Culture

By Aaron H. Esman, M.D. New York/Oxford: Columbia University Press, 1990. 118 pp.

Carl Adatto

Carl Adatto

Carl P. Adatto
NEW ORLEANS

Carl Adatto  

This book is one of a series on Psychoanalysis and Culture; it focuses on the interrelationship between culture and adolescent development. Esman, an experienced analyst of adolescents, reviews the history of concepts about adolescents' place in society and presents his view that the adolescent acts as a shaper and barometer of culture. In developing his thesis, he disagrees with the concept of a "generation gap" between adolescent and adult society. He contends that the adolescent reflects what is occurring in society. He believes that currently held concepts such as "moratorium," idealism, and Sturm und Drang, are not not necessarily observed in all adolescents.

In his chapter, "Culture as Shaper of Adolescence," he states that social scientists view the phenomenology of adolescence as in large measure culturally determined. However, by placing emphasis on the effects of industrialization and consumerism on current adolescent behavior and customs, he seems to simplify the society in which we live. Anorexia nervosa is cited as a dramatic demonstration of the impact of culture and cultural change on adolescents of many social and class backgrounds. While cultural ideals influence body configuration, it is questionable how ubiquitous anorexia is, because large segments of our culture are indifferent to the ideal of a thin person—not to mention those suffering from hunger and starvation.

In the chapter, "The New Sexuality," clinical examples demonstrate how his patients dealt with their psychic conflicts as distinct from current social sexual patterns. He contends that the so-called sexual revolution seems to be a change of cultural patterns with which most adolescents are comfortable and that only the most vulnerable adolescents require "the ultimate redress of personality disintegration and ego regression" (p. 78) in coping with the new sexuality. In like manner, he addresses the problems of AIDS and adolescent pregnancy as having little or marginal effect on adolescent sexual conduct.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Image and Insight. Essays in Psychoanalysis and the Arts

By Ellen Handler Spitz. New York: Columbia University Press, 1991. 273 pp.

Aaron Esman

Aaron Esman

Aaron H. Esman
NEW YORK

Aaron Esman  

In her first book, Art & Psyche,1 Ellen Handler Spitz, a psychoanalytically trained art historian, performed the great service of outlining with clarity and penetration the several ways in which psychoanalysis has been used to illuminate the lives of artists, works of art, and the processes of both creativity and aesthetic response. The present volume brings together a dozen essays of varying length and depth on a number of aspects of the cultural scene, ranging from classic Greek drama to subway graffiti, in which she demonstrates once again the sharpness of her critical faculty and the scope of her command both of psychoanalytic ideas and of cultural phenomena.

Spitz's ambition is substantial. The first essay in this collection, "Looking and Longing," aims at nothing less than the formulation of a psychoanalytic aesthetics, i.e., the restoration of the notion of pleasure into aesthetic discourse. Spitz is impatient with the austere formalism that, she finds, has come to dominate art-historical and art-critical theory; she wishes to emphasize the role of the object in evoking or resonating with the viewer's desire, in filling a lack or restoring a felt loss in the viewer's unconscious life. Freud's dictum that the finding of an object is actually a refinding applies, then, in the realm of aesthetics as it does in "real" life. The paradox here—that many art objects appear to evoke aesthetic responses in individuals with widely varying life experiences (and, therefore, "desire" structures)—is not fully explored, but Spitz's concept would presumably imply "panhuman" needs/lack/desires.

Or, at least, within a particular culture. This point is germane to Spitz's essay on African sculpture, which she speaks of as "Charged Objects"—charged, that is, with intense spiritual meanings specific to the culture in and for which they were created. She addresses here the oft-argued issue of the possibility of meaningful response to such objects detached or uprooted from their cultural context.

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray  

The authors observe that many men view combat as a positive event in their lives. They postulate that individuals who suffer from chronic post-traumatic stress disorder maintain their symptoms because these perpetuate the memory of rewarding, intense wartime experiences. This often inhibits adaptation to peacetime circumstances. The average Vietnam era soldiers were between 17 and 23 years of age. These young people formed warrior identities before they consolidated a mature sense of self. Combat circumstances required them to depend on their group for survival; phase-appropriate autonomy was deferred. They were repatriated to a society that rejected and devalued Vietnam combatants and offered no positive mirroring experiences. Most frequently, the authors believe, psychotherapists reflected similar values as well as idiosyncratic anti-war biases. These professionals focused on the negative combat experiences and failed to validate the positive, adaptive aspects of the veteran's warrior personality. Thus, they could not help their patients grow into coherent, independent, mature human beings.

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray  

The case of Osheroff v. Chestnut Lodge focused attention on the relationship between pharmacotherapy and dynamic psychotherapy in the treatment of mood disorders. The author presents a group of representative case vignettes under the headings: the impact of pharmacotherapy on the psychotherapist's attitude and technique, the effect of pharmacotherapy on psychotherapy, the impact of pharmacotherapy on the patient, and the decision to combine modalities. He concludes that multimodal treatment is increasingly becoming the norm. The evaluating clinician needs to accept the burden of documenting the decision to include or to omit medication in a great many cases. It is important to use medication and psychotherapy in an informed and systematic fashion, rather than introducing either only after the other fails. Medication may be prescribed by the psychotherapist or by a different treater.

The Abstinence of the Psychoanalyst. Riva Novey, Pp. 344-362.

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray

Sheila Gray  

Structural theory requires us to distinguish between psychoanalytic neutrality (equidistance from id, ego, and superego) and abstinence, a concept that refers to drive gratification. In the process of mastering the frustration engendered by abstinence, the patient develops a mature sense of reality. Competent psychoanalysts continuously assess and regulate the expression of abstinence to promote the emergence and interpretation of the transference neurosis, remembering that they invited their patients to discover and reveal wishes that will be disappointed. These clinicians must unremittingly confront and master their desires and frustrations in order to approach patients with empathy and alliance and to avoid countertransference enactments. The author offers three detailed illustrations of the management of cases that test the clinician's capacity to maintain a psychoanalytic attitude. Two also illustrate the process of cultivating the requisite technical skills in supervision. There is an extensive but focused literature review.

690

Berke differentiates "benign psychosis" from "malignant psychosis," which is an invasive, life-destructive phenomenon. Envy, greed, and jealousy are the aggressive forces that underlie malignant psychosis. The essential symbols of life—the breast, the womb, and the penis—are attacked by malign, psychotic aspects of the self, and both inner and outer realities become persecutory. Berke presents clinical examples of how these persecutory forces operate and how the destructive consequences can be opposed by life-affirming counterparts—gratitude, generosity, and compassion.

695

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

The working alliance is a problematic concept in regard to its utility, definition, and relationship to transference. Rawn believes the notion of working alliance is unavoidable because "implicit in our theory of therapy is the idea that effective interpretation leads to structural change when a nonconflicted part of the patient is able to use it." He defines the working alliance as "that part of the patient's relationship to the analyst triggered by the patient's observing ego that is totally devoid of transference." Although clinically there is overlap of working alliance and transference, the concepts can be separated. When a patient associates freely with minimal resistance or assimilates interpretations into insights, the patient has formed a working alliance. Working in therapy should not be confused with internalization of the therapeutic object. The alliance is an ego function: "that part of the ego that has to do with observation, synthesis, and acceptance of accurate interpretation.

698

Imagination and the Unconscious: A Critique of the Neo-Romantic Program. M. D. Faber, Pp. 437-457.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

Faber critiques the work of Owen Barfield and James Hillman, leaders of a "school of imagination." Their theoretical position is derived from the writings of Wordsworth and Coleridge from whom they have revived Romantic imagination as a panacea to combat the materialism of modern scientific thinking. Faber re-examines the works of Wordsworth and Coleridge and arrives at an understanding of imagination different from that usually described. Wordsworth reads into the world a relational warmth that is derived from the "mirror relationship" between mother and child. However, Wordsworth fails to perceive the internalized "bad" stimulation due to childhood separation and frustrations. Wordsworth substitutes both imagination and nature for the relinquished parental object. Coleridge, too, substitutes imagination for the lost object and provides insight into the "bad" side of that relationship. He gives a projected version of his own unhappy existence.

Barfield embraces an imagination that has the power to overcome the void of the modern world through comforting images. Hillman decries analyzing the imagination away and views psychopathology as a way to salvation. Both Barfield and Hillman miss the fact that imagination "bears witness not to the divine, beatific nature of human personality once it has escaped the idol of scientific thought or reason … (but) bears witness … to the split, agonized nature of our fundamental years.

699

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

The author draws from Kohut's concepts of self and selfobject to examine the therapeutic changes that occurred during the therapy of a twenty-eight-year-old woman suffering from "a profound disturbance in her capacity to feel alive." The patient had a need "to establish a bond with another person in order to support an extremely tenuous inner experience," and in doing so lost her individuality. In the course of therapy the unmarried patient became pregnant, and the pregnancy became a critical time in the therapy. The patient kept the child and later brought the infant to her therapy sessions. The author did not evaluate the patient's decisions, but maintained "interested attention to subjective process," with a focus on the patient's autonomy. In the course of therapy there was a progressive consolidation and firming of the patient's self-structure; she saw herself as a center of initiative and volition and was able to express her needs and wishes to others. Wolfe believes that patients may attempt to strengthen and differentiate their self-experience through relationship with the therapist, and that transference is a necessary condition for maintaining or restoring the self-experience.

699

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

McWilliams's thesis is that "analysts subtly convey two complementary messages that are essential to a therapeutic outcome." Analysts indicate devotion to the patient's welfare, which is experienced as a soothing kind of maternal joining. Analysts

699

also embody integrity, which is experienced as a stimulating kind of paternal separateness. The maternal type of interpretation holds and soothes the patient while encouraging the patient to attend to painful ideas. The paternal type of intervention confronts the patient as a responsible person capable of accepting painful ideas. These two types of analytic positions are examined in detail, and used to describe therapeutic failures and technical implications in regard to degree of pathology, type of pathology, and interminability of analysis.

700

Nathan Schlessinger

Nathan Schlessinger  

In the preface to Volume 3 of this series, the editor repeats his indictment of psychoanalysis as a scientific theory, quoting critics who describe it as a set of unconfirmed hypotheses, with a literature of self-congratulatory clinical histories and a history of extravagant claims of efficacy in treatment. He sets forth the clinician's compelling reliance on intensive investigation of individuals and disparagement of empirical research as irrelevant to clinical theory. Apparently, in the editor's view, the typical psychoanalyst would disregard or ignore the fact that theory instructs therapist and patient, that the analyst influences the process through gross and subtle communication, and that patients learn to speak the language of their analyst, whatever his or her theoretical persuasion. He quotes Holt to the effect that uncontrolled clinical case studies are devoid of scientific value except as a source of hypotheses. Yet he acknowledges that very little of interest and very few creative ideas have been generated in laboratory studies of personality.

Freud at the Crossroads

By Alexander Grinstein, M.D. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, Inc., 1990. 612 pp.

Calvern Narcisi

Calvern Narcisi

Calvern E. Narcisi
DENVER, CO

Calvern Narcisi  

In this book Grinstein extends the methodology he used in his earlier work, On Sigmund Freud's Dreams.1 The present work is a clinical book that reads like a psychoanalysis. As Grinstein states in his Introduction, he utilizes "a fundamental tenet of psychoanalysis: the principle of strict psychic determinism, that all associations are meaningful" (p. 3).

The subject of the analysis is Freud, between the years 1892 and 1906. Grinstein defines these years as "the crossroads" for several reasons. During this period, Freud was in the midst of his self-analysis and therefore in the most intense throes of his relationship with Fliess. In addition, during this time Freud discovered the importance of infantile fantasy and abandoned the seduction hypothesis as his unitary theory of neurosis.

Although Grinstein states that it is not his intention to analyze Freud, it is the very fact that Freud's associations are dealt with analytically that makes this biography so fascinating. The book focuses on seven of Freud's dreams, four literary references that Freud made in letters to Fliess, and ten "good" books which Freud listed in response to a questionnaire by Hugo Heller.

The book is arranged chronologically.

James Edgar  

Bernstein discusses some of the elements contributing to motivation for psychoanalysis, factors that foster this motivation, and psychotherapy as a preliminary step. He feels this preparatory work helps the patient to control anxiety about unconscious wishes and to establish a sense of safety about the analytic situation. He does not feel that there have to be any contraindications to converting from psychotherapy to psychoanalysis with the same analyst, as long as this possibility was considered by the analyst upon beginning treatment. Several case vignettes are presented to illustrate his hypothesis. Factors identified as important in fostering the development of motivation are: the influence of the recommendation of analysis, an internal focus of distress, recognition of limitations caused by neurotic misery, the parallel of fears in life and fears in treatment, some comfort with analytic regression, dissatisfactions with the limitations of psychotherapy, and a desire to intensify the treatment.

Alan Pollack  

Four concise and exceptionally clear reports of psychoanalytic treatment are presented in this volume, each one accompanied by two commentaries written by respected, senior analysts. The overall effect is a portrait of mainstream American psychoanalysis as it is practiced and as it is understood by its practitioners.

The first case report is a small gem by Rudolph Loewenstein, entitled "The Old Woman's Touch: Reflections on the Treatment of a Case of Obsessional Neurosis." In the 1930's, Loewenstein took over the analysis of a woman nearly paralyzed by obsessional fear of contamination from the touch of an old servant woman who had been briefly in her employ. In psychiatric nosology, the woman suffered from a severe case of obsessive-compulsive disorder, complete with the familiar elements of extreme doubting, compulsive washing, and semimagical rituals, such as covering her bed (and the analytic couch!) with tissue. Contradicting today's popular biological reductionism, however, the disorder was both precipitated and cured by psychoanalysis.

Katharine Rees  

This essay presents a very clear rationale for the adaptations of technique necessary to accomplish intermediate aims and strengthen the therapeutic alliance, on the way toward achieving the long-term aim of intrapsychic structural change. Such carefully thought out adaptations have evolved from a broader model of development influencing our understanding of process and outcome. Child analysis has contributed much, though such adaptations are also central to analytic work with more disturbed adults.

Intermediate aims are tailored according to each child's stage of cognitive and ego development. But also, since few patients have only a clear-cut childhood neurosis, the intermediate aims can address developmental lags and distortions, an admixture of interpretation and ego support known as "developmental help." Two very interesting examples are given of this delicate and sensitive process—with a four-year-old boy who first needed help in feeling safe, and a sexually promiscuous adolescent girl who needed some response to her affectional needs and fragile sense of self. This could then be followed by more thorough interpretation of unconscious conflict and defense.

Diary of a Baby

By Daniel N. Stern, M.D. New York: Basic Books, Inc., 1990. 165 pp.

Anne Erreich

Anne Erreich

Anne Erreich
NEW YORK

Anne Erreich  

This book is likely to please new parents, though it will be viewed more cautiously by psychoanalysts.

Diary of a Baby is a natural progression from Stern's earlier books, The First Relationship (Harvard University Press, 1977) and The Interpersonal World of the Infant (Basic Books, 1985). Combining elements of each of those, Diary of a Baby is directed at a lay audience and draws on both observational and experimental data for the purpose of inferring the infant's subjective experience and her growing sense of self and intersubjectivity.

The book is structured in the form of fictional diary entries at five critical epochs in an infant's life: the "World of Feelings" (at six weeks), the "Immediate Social World" (at four and one-half months), the "World of Mindscapes" (at twelve months), the "World of Words" (at twenty months), and the "World of Stories" (at four years). Each chapter begins with an overview of that developmental phase, followed by three views of an ordinary event in the life of a child at that age (e.g., at six weeks, observing a patch of sunlight; at twelve months, momentarily straying too far from mother; at four years, snuggling with parents in bed and helping mother prepare breakfast). For each event, Stern provides, first, a brief description of it, second, a putative "diary" entry, i.e., Stern's speculations regarding the infant's experience of the event rendered in highly evocative, impressionistic language, and finally, Stern's gloss on the episode in light of infant research.

Stern deserves credit for this creative and integrative approach, and for his continuing efforts to bridge the gap between the observed infant and the experiencing infant. His pioneering efforts to integrate research in developmental psychology with clinical issues are most accessible to parents in this book. Stern manages to introduce such notions as free association, identification and superego functioning, fantasy, displacement, transitional objects, and intersubjectivity without labeling them, but in a manner that conveys a sense of these mental functions. Finally, he provides an excellent annotated selective bibliography for expanded reading.
