[[RunningHead]]

Psychoanalytic Knowledge

By Eugene B. Brody. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, Inc., 1990. 246 pp.

Ronald Fleischmann

Ronald Fleischmann

Ronald Fleischmann
DALLAS, TX

Ronald Fleischmann  

Psychoanalytic Knowledge is an ambitious attempt to challenge the fundamental concepts of the theory of psychoanalysis. In the past decade, there has been an increasing interest in the basis of psychoanalytic evidence, the theory of scientific knowledge, and our

495

understanding of the psychoanalytic process. Brody has brought together his psychoanalytic and sociocultural understanding of the subject to define, re-examine, challenge, and offer alternative hypotheses to what we have come to know as psychoanalytic theory. The book is not easy reading. It should be reserved for serious students of the subject who have a sincere interest in examining fundamental theoretical issues. There are few clinical references and most of these are anthropologic, although they do add compelling data to the arguments.

Brody's approach is to lay out his basic understanding of psychoanalysis (as a clinical treatment, a scientific research modality, and a contribution toward developing a general psychology) and to place it in a cultural, economic context. The repeated observation is that the field of study, the individual, is influenced by the observer. In the last chapter of the book, in which he examines the convergence of psychoanalysis and anthropology, similar observations are made regarding the role of the ethnologist. The effect is often jarring. It leaves one doubting what we have come to understand as readily explainable psychic and societal phenomena in terms of our conventional theory. In a very interesting chapter, Brody examines the education of the psychoanalyst, who is influenced by the subculture into which he gains inclusion, and the effects of this on how he functions as a clinician and scientist.

This approach paves the way for the major thesis of the work. Mainly citing the writings of the anthropologist, Edward Sapir, and the linguist, Ferdinand de Saussure, Brody seeks to alter and redefine both topographic and structural theory. He sees the concept of drive theory as unnecessary. In addition, he prefers to replace the concept of unconscious with that of preconscious. He views the mind as an information processor and makes analogy to computer terminology. Since the concept of ego requires the idea of repression as an active force removing unaccceptable ideas from consciousness, he would dispense with the structural concept altogether in favor of selection and avoidance. In its place Brody would see the analytic process as an examination of self-deception through the exploration of the unconscious/preconscious. In particular, he pays attention to the relationship and the communications between the observer and the observed.

The Psychoanalytic Review. LXXVIII, 1991

A Reconsideration of the Freud-Tausk-Deutsch Relationship. James W. Hamilton. Pp. 267-278.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

Hamilton re-examines the complexities of Freud's analysis of Helene Deutsch who was in analysis with Freud at the same time she was analyzing Victor Tausk. Hamilton postulates that Freud's guilt about the death of his infant brother Julius caused countertransference problems. For Freud, Deutsch's preoccupation with Tausk recreated the situation of vying for the attention of a woman interested in another man. Hamilton suggests that Freud was unconsciously angered that Deutsch allowed herself to be captivated by Tausk, and because of the anxiety over revived death wishes, he forced Deutsch to terminate her analysis of Tausk. Freud's conflict of sibling rivalry and early object loss had been intensified by the child's belief in the omnipotence of thought. The author also considers that these issues had an important influence on Freud's formulation of the death instinct.

The Psychoanalytic Review. LXXVIII, 1991

The Text/Body Connection: Character as Fetish inThe Plumed Serpent. Marcia Ian. Pp. 279-300.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

Ian compares D. H. Lawrence's and Freud's concepts of the unconscious. In contrast to Freud, freedom for Lawrence lies not with consciousness but with unimpeded expression. Drawing on Lacanian theory, Ian examines The Plumed Serpent in detail. In the novel, Lawrence created "a religion of the unconscious in which characters solemnly ritualize their own symbolic embodiment." The "drive to representation," the expression of the unconscious, is so intense in The Plumed Serpent as to become "a literary pathology" manifesting itself as obsessive acts and fetishism. The author states that "if The Plumed Serpent is a ritual of embodiment, then in it character plays the role of fetish." The characters embody and represent the phallus. The novel is "a symbolic ritual of loss and reconstitution whose aim is not only to deny and asseverate the loss of the phallus, but ultimately to expand a two-sided relationship into a three-sided one." "In language, metaphor and fiction, Lawrence sacrifices and reconstitutes … his own symbolic phallus." Ian concludes that Lawrence unites the signified and the signifier in such a way that they will never be put asunder.

Gender Stereotyping in Supervisory Styles. Jennifer Leighton. Pp. 347-363.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

The author draws on theories of male and female development proposed by Gilligan and Chodorow to examine masculine and feminine styles of supervision. On the masculine end of the supervisory spectrum is the extreme scientific position; at the feminine end is the extreme intuitive position. The author details these styles and provides clinical examples. She states that the masculine style is overvalued in our culture, that both styles in their extremes may be deleterious, and that a balance between them is needed for effective supervision.

The Psychoanalytic Review. LXXVIII, 1991

The Addiction to Negativity. Robert C. Lane; James W. Hull; Leonore M. Foehrenbach. Pp. 391-401.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

Patients exposed to intense negativity during early life may develop an addiction to negative experience as adolescents and adults. This may become the central organizing feature of their personalities. Manifestations of early negativity include anhedonia, attachment to physical pain, fear of success, masochism, deprivation of self and others, and searching only for the negative. The dynamic function of negativity can involve a desire for revenge against the caretakers from infancy who were sources of deprivation and frustration. In addition, negativity can serve a defensive function by expressing through projective-introjective mechanisms, as well as warding off, dangerous wishes to merge. Countertransference reactions frequently appear in treatment and their resolution is crucial. Patient and therapist must investigate the adaptive functions of extreme negativity to resolve this symptom.

698

Pornography and the Primal Scene: A Report on the Voyage to Brobdingnag. Charles A. Peterson. Pp. 411-424.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

The author describes a patient who suffered recurrent primal scene exposure in childhood, and later developed an addiction to big-screen pornography. In the patient's preference for large image pornography, he would take himself as an object, perceiving himself as small in relation to the giant phalluses on the screen. In addition to the attempt to master the primal scene trauma, the patient attempted to create a potent father and augment his own masculine identity through incorporation and collation of various part-objects.

Analytic Time. R. M. Waugaman. Pp. 29-47.

Lee Grossman

Lee Grossman

Lee Grossman  

Waugaman uses brief examples from his practice and from the literature to show how the temporal aspects of the treatment setting may reactivate the impact of childhood events. In some of the vignettes, feelings associated with separation, loss, or rivalry emerged when the duration of the treatment matched the patient's age at the time of the birth of a sibling. Some patients experience fantasies and feelings associated with birth in the ninth month of treatment. Some patients experience the therapists's schedule of patients as reflecting birth order. Reactions to beginning treatment or to termination may reveal fantasies of birth or death. "Anniversary reactions" are a further example of the phenomena Waugaman considers. He speculates on the development of time sense, emphasizing the role of separation experiences within the symbiotic dyad.

The Analyst's Stance and the Method of Free Association. Anton O. Kris. Pp. 25-41.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Kris offers a review, partly historical, partly a presentation of his own view, of several aspects of the "stance," including the analyst's neutrality; the nature of transference and how it is treated by the analyst; and interpretation. His views are practical and helpful. He describes two quite different understandings of transference: as a re-creation of an old relationship, or as expressing all the patient's unconscious fantasies, those from the past and those arising from present problems. The confusion of these two ideas causes trouble to the analyst.

Kris also writes about divergent and convergent conflict. What is especially striking in the paper is his discussion of Kohut's ideas; Kris believes Kohut's tolerant attitude toward the patient can help the patient sufficiently to overcome shame to be able to work on self-critical thoughts. An "affirmative attitude," meaning careful avoidance of anything that might seem critical of the patient, permits the narcissistic patient to deal with the sense of entitlement.

The Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XLV, 1990

The Third Individuation: The Effect of Biological Parenthood on Separation-Individuation Processes in Adulthood. Calvin A. Colarusso. Pp. 179-194.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Colarusso suggests that the two "individuations" described by Mahler and Blos are followed by a third, which occurs in "early" (20 to 40 years) and "middle" (40 to 60 years) adulthood. He discusses the events that bring it about: acquisition of a sexual partner; the births of children; the changes in parent-child relationships as these children grow up. Problems occur along the way, such as loneliness in the young

341

adult after becoming distanced from a parent but as yet without an important new love object. Colarusso discusses how the whole process is affected by events, such as the arrival of children and the working-out of a new relationship between the young or middle adult and the parents. Oedipal resolution, for example, proceeds further. Colarusso briefly mentions the possibility that a further individuation later occurs.

Some cases illustrate Colarusso's exposition. The paper is likely to add to our understanding of late adolescence and early and middle adulthood; it will help our treatment of patients in those years.

342

The Psychoanalytic Study of the Child. XLV, 1990

The Analysis of a Latency Boy: The Developmental Impact of Separation, Divorce, and Remarriage. Audrey Gavshon. Pp. 217-233.

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain

Gerard Fountain  

Gavshon offers a clear and convincing account of the treatment of a child whose parents were divorced and thereafter appeared at times to want him and at others to reject him for new partners. The child, nine and one half when his analysis began, was unusually articulate, able to express his feelings and examine their origins and meanings. We can learn much of great practical value from his treatment. For example, he overcame a school difficulty with adding decimals when it was suggested to him that the trouble was related to his inability to know where he was (he moved back and forth between his parents) or whom he was going to lose.

In her conclusion, however, Gavshon seems to offer insights not fully supported by the material she has presented. Her paper is nevertheless a well-written and instructive account.

342

Miller examines Freud's 1891 monograph, On Aphasia, and finds that Freud's neurophysiology anticipates many of his later psychoanalytic concepts. Freud did not accept the then-current model of point-for-point projection of body parts or functions onto the cerebral cortex, but formulated a "non-localizationist" position. Freud utilized a dynamic rather than static view of brain functioning. On Aphasia

Incest "Rediscovered." Shirley Panken. Pp. 547-565.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

Panken criticizes Louise DeSalvo's book, Virginia Woolf: The Impact of Childhood Sexual Abuse on Her Life and Work. Panken disputes DeSalvo's major contention that "sexual violence" by Woolf's half-brothers, Gerald and George Duckworth, is a central theme in her writing and had a serious impact on her psychopathology. This sexual exploitation was "neither annihilating nor instrumental in leading to her early suicide attempt or to her suicide." The author states that the important factors in Woolf's suicide were her cyclothymic predisposition, characterological depression, decreased self-esteem, fear of losing her writing ability, and a loss of closeness in her intimate relationships.

"One's Effort to Find a Little Truth": Ethel Schwabacher's Artistic and Psychoanalytic Odyssey. Jeffrey Berman. Pp. 607-627.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

Ethel Schwabacher, best known as a painter, turned to writing when she became incapacitated with arthritis. In her journal, The Tortoise and the Angel, she wrote extensively of her experience in psychoanalysis. Schwabacher suffered from low self-esteem and depression, attempting suicide several times. She was in treatment for two and one half years with Helene Deutsch, and then for nearly thirty years with Marianne Kris. Berman documents similarities between Schwabacher and the patient described in Deutsch's published case titled "Hysterical Fate Neurosis." Psychoanalysis enabled Schwabacher to discover many of the causes of her conflicts and offered her an explanatory system that she used in her artistic work. Berman believes the benefit of treatment was due not primarily to insight, but to the therapeutic alliance with Kris.

Psychodynamic Psychiatry: Theory and Practice, Volumes I & II

By John Frosch, M.D. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, Inc., 1990. 864 pp.

Harriet Wolfe

Harriet Wolfe

Harriet L. Wolfe
SAN FRANCISCO

Harriet Wolfe  

In this two-volume work John Frosch undertakes the ambitious task of laying out the psychodynamic foundation of general psychiatry. Volume I is devoted largely to defining principles of psychodynamic formulation. The end of Volume I and all of Volume II present a survey of psychiatric clinical disorders and attempt to explicate the psychodynamic factors essential to each. In this era of descriptive psychiatry, when psychodynamic theory and practice are commonly devalued in residency training, this work is a landmark attempt to fill an important need: to salvage the skills and wisdom necessary to understand and treat the whole patient.

There are many high points in these two volumes and there are also some problems. Probably the richest element of the two volumes is Frosch's ability to present excellent critical and synthetic reviews of the history of psychoanalytic theory and practice. A wonderful example is his chapter on character disorders. The DSM-III-R definition of personality traits is contrasted with the evolution of the concept of character in psychoanalytic thinking. (Frosch elects to use the terms "personality" and "character" interchangeably.) One recognizes, on reading this lucid, thorough, discerning synthesis, that the author was an active participant in the unfolding of theory and practice.

Clinical vignettes are another extremely valuable aspect of the work. One becomes acquainted with several of Frosch's patients if one reads straight through because some of them are used several times to make relevant points. The "pigeon lady" (my term) serves as an elegant example of phobic behavior in Volume I (p. 346) and as an example of zoophilia in Volume II (p. 603). Pearls of clinical wisdom, such as the association of severe obsessive-compulsive symptomatology in latency with schizophrenia at a later age (p. 357), are also plentiful. They enrich our knowledge of the phenomenology of mental illness and they can be filed away for future use.

Immaterial Facts. Freud's Discovery of Psychic Reality and Klein's Development of his Work

By Robert Caper, M.D. Northvale, NJ: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1988. 266 pp.

Aaron Esman

Aaron Esman

Aaron H. Esman
NEW YORK

Aaron Esman  

The negative views of Freudian orthodoxy notwithstanding, Melanie Klein, along with her followers, always believed that she was the

653

true heir to Freud's scientific legacy. Although her ideas have achieved wide recognition and support in much of the psychoanalytic world, they have gained little acceptance in the United States. At most, grudging acknowledgment of the value of her explorations of preoedipal development has accompanied general skepticism about her theoretical system and her technical approaches.

In this clearly written book, Caper, an analyst of adults and children in California, attempts to validate the Kleinian claim, by presenting in language accessible to both lay and professional readers the evolution and theoretical foundations of Freud's thought and, in sequence, how in Caper's view Klein's concepts have built upon, extended, and/or corrected them. Caper's retelling of Freud's intellectual progress from (in Sulloway's terms) "biologist of the mind" to a more truly psychological conception of its development, function, and structure is lucid, accurate, scholarly, and fair-minded. It would serve well as a text for beginning students (and, indeed, as a refresher for those who are more advanced). His emphasis throughout is on Freud's evolving construction of the notion of "psychic reality" and its centrality in the shaping of consciousness. Using Little Hans as his test case, he shows how Freud's ideas were progressively remodeled as clinical data required this, and how, ultimately, his revision of the theory of anxiety led him to new insights about aggression as well.

When he proceeds to set forth Klein's contributions, however, Caper tends to slip from the role of historian to that of advocate. Though Freud was capable (or even culpable) of error, Klein apparently was not. Her reformulations of early development, her concepts of "phantasy," her complex picture of early projective and introjective processes, her acceptance of the notion of the death instinct, her attribution to the infant of elaborate cognitive capacities and innate knowledge, her unquestioned assumption of the equivalence of childhood play and adult free association—none of these is subject to any question, none seems to require any evidential support beyond Klein's clinical experience and, apparently, her infallible judgment. In the early controversy regarding child analysis between Klein and Anna Freud, Klein is represented as unfailingly correct and Anna Freud as the defender of a "stunted" view of its potentialities.

By Peter B. Neubauer, M.D. and Alexander Neubauer. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley Publishing Company, Inc., 1990. 223 pp.

Mervyn Peskin

Mervyn Peskin

Mervyn M. Peskin
NEW YORK

Mervyn Peskin  

The Neubauers, father and son, psychoanalyst and writer, take us on a trip to the ever-turbulent but vital realm of the nature-nurture interface. This, as they say, "is a book about accepting into one's life

668

both hereditary history (nature) and environmental history (nurture) as interactive parts of human individuality" (p. 9). The book reads as a guide for thinking about children, family, patients, ourselves—a guide that stresses the currently unrespectable contribution of genetic endowment to development and adaptation. Reminding us that unrelated strangers differ in only six million of the six billion base pairs of DNA in human chromosomes, full siblings in only two million and identical twins in none at all, the authors highlight the scope for variation and individuality conferred by the differences while focusing on the powerful significance of the genetic givens. This is the theme that, not surprisingly, dominates the book, as it does all cogent discourse on the matter. However, as the Neubauers point out, except in cases of extreme pathology, it does not inform much of current thinking about development and behavior.

How, they ask, has the popular conception of development come to focus so exclusively on learning and experience over heredity even as new information about the gene explodes around us? The reasons are many. There is a worthwhile historical review tracing the conflicting ideas of the importance of innate versus environmental factors in Rationalist as opposed to Enlightenment thinkers right through to late nineteenth, early twentieth century scientific thought, with an emphasis on the terrible misuses to which extremes of either philosophy have been put in recent times. The racism of Social Darwinism and the "justification" of genocide realized in the Holocaust, based on genetic stereotyping, have left an overwhelming and understandable cloud. At the same time, attempts to form "truly equal societies," in which environmental factors were given all the blame and all the hope of eliminating greed and competitiveness, have also proven destructive to millions. However, it is the former, the fear of genetic determinism, that currently looms large over the discourse. On a more individual level, the authors point out that children come into the world as genetic entities unto themselves more than is comfortable to admit. The narcissistic wishes of parents will incline against seeing this. While there is something healthy and necessary in this narcissistic inclusiveness, recognizing each child's individual temperament and individual pace of maturation, as well as tolerating differences, is crucial to the development of the child as unique.

Written by Lou Salomé in 1934, a few years before her death, this is neither autobiography nor comprehensive history. To gain a perspective on her, including her relationship with Freud, one must look to other sources (especially Pfeiffer's collection of the Freud-Salomé correspondence1). She was an accomplished author, the friend and confidante of Nietzsche, later Rilke's lover, and an active member of various European intellectual circles. According to Gay, she was "brilliant, attractive, knowledgeable and productive"; "a grand dame, a collector of philosophers and poets." He describes her as "spectacular and seductive, a powerful, voluptuous figure, with an appetite for men, especially brilliant ones."2

Sheila Gray  

There is growing evidence of substantial clinical heterogeneity in neurotic depression. In a prospective follow-up study, the author and co-workers found recurrent major depression or bipolar disorder in 40% of cases that had been diagnosed neurotic depression. Others suffered from chronic dysthymia or subclinical mood disorders. These patients present with neurotic, narcissistic, or existential concerns. Clinicians who are disinclined to use medication tend to focus on the psychological aspects of the condition; but failure to recognize and treat the core affective pathology leads to a therapeutic impasse in many cases. The patient who does not recover may then be misdiagnosed as borderline. Some physicians rely excessively on tricyclic antidepressants, and tend to label patients who do not respond to this one pharmacological modality as treatment-resistant or characterological depressives. Cases of chronic depression fell into the categories of residual major depression, anxious or atypical depression, and dysthymic disorder. The latter includes cases of subaffective dysthymia and character-spectrum depressive disorder. The author offers suggestions for diagnosing and treating these ostensibly hopeless conditions. There is a comprehensive, sophisticated bibliography.

Sheila Gray  

Psychoanalysts must determine whether their patients' belief systems serve normative or neurotic goals. The author finds that hysterical patients seem drawn to religious systems that foster intense emotional experience and irrational belief. Obsessional and depressive individuals tend to seek perfectionism in their religious practice. The former search for logical, correct solutions to existential problems; their religious thought is characterized by dogmatism and doubt. Depressive individuals may express their incapacity to achieve perfection in beliefs of their inherent evil or sinfulness; they feel judged and condemned. Narcissistic patients share psychopathological traits with their depressive and obsessional peers. In addition, they often exhibit attitudes of religious superiority, sometimes veiled by a depressive constellation. Patients often translate masochistic attitudes into religious practices; these are prominent in Christians who identify with the suffering Christ in the belief that that is the path to divine love. Paranoid individuals tend to be authoritarian in their outlook, focusing on control and power. This attracts them to strong leaders and inspires hostility toward those who hold different beliefs. There are several lucid clinical illustrations.

Melford E. Spiro, the psychoanalytic anthropologist to whom this volume is dedicated, describes his own intellectual development in exploring the relationship between culture and human nature. Spiro has done fieldwork in the Ojibwa, Ifaluk, Israeli kibbutz, and Burmese societies. From this work he has concluded, in contrast to previous anthropological theorizing, that culture is not the exclusive determinant of personality and that personality is not exclusively the internalization of culture. He argues that the Freudian structural model offers a more complex view of personality as independent of behavior and culture. He also argues that this conceptualization of aspects of personality in conflict with culture offers a fuller explanation of observable facts. He uses his research on aggression to document these assertions about a pancultural human nature.

The author discusses the trickster figure in North American mythology in terms of duality of function. The trickster is both a polymorphously sexual buffoon and a heroic cultural innovator. Manson critically assesses Carroll's attempt to integrate Freud's theory of culture with Lévi-Strauss's structural analysis of the trickster as representing the dichotomous structure of mythical thought. Manson, in contrast, argues that sublimation is the mediating conceptual link that unifies the polarized personalities of the trickster. He concludes that the change from sybarite to culture hero represents the problem of ego development in psychosocial maturation.

Erroneous interpretation of Freud has occurred because psychologist-historians use common sense to test their theories and do not consult relevant documents. Eissler advocates the principle of "unrestricted exegesis" moving into "psychoanalytic common sense," i.e., a set of working hypotheses held in common by psychoanalysts. An analogy is examined and preconscious or unconscious imagery is reconstructed. Content may be interpreted in all possible directions: literal, literary, personal, historical, and symbolic. It "may be looked at as a day residue, as a derivative of a repressed impulse, as a biographical element, as a referent to a historical event, or as if it were part of a legend, fairy tale, or as an archaic symbol derived from any area of culture, religion, art, and so on." Eissler cautions, however, of the danger of overinterpretation.

The Psychoanalytic Review. LXXVIII, 1991

Issues in the Psychoanalytic Treatment of Single Females over Thirty. Janice S. Lieberman. Pp. 177-198.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

Psychoanalysis with women patients over thirty, who seek marriage and children as a goal, can pose particular problems. Lieberman criticizes the position that an unwanted single status is the result of neurotic conflict. She states that this problem may not be just intrapsychic; reality factors are important and must also be addressed. Three clinical examples are given, and transference, countertransference, resistance, and defense are examined. Lieberman postulates and describes a "singles syndrome." She concludes that when intrapsychic change occurs as a result of treatment, one may hope that external reality will change; however, one can lead a full life without marriage.

[[RunningHead]]

The Psychoanalytic Review. LXXVIII, 1991

Conrad's Dream of a Common Language: Lacan and "The Secret Sharer." Joyce Wexler. Pp. 599-606.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

Wexler uses Conrad's story, "The Secret Sharer," to explicate Lacan's theory of "the subject's entry into the symbolic order." A Lacanian reading can account for both the story's rhetorical success and its limits. At the story's conclusion, the captain,

700

unable to gain mastery through the symbolic order, learns to imitate Leggart, his double whom he envies, by regressing to the preverbal mirror stage (the imaginary order) where he can more fully identify with the other. Conrad considered "The Secret Sharer," in which the written words fully conveyed his perception, a rare success in achieving full communication with the reader. However, the successful communication which the story describes is not at the verbal level. In the climactic scene, when the captain and Leggart perfectly understand each other's meaning, words are primarily reduced to gesture. The author concludes that Conrad's dream of a "common language" uniting reader and writer is impossible. "The Secret Sharer" demonstrates that complete communication can occur only with a double, and never by means of language.

701

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Society of New England, East

November 4, 1991. SOME NUCLEAR CONFLICTS OF THE INFANTILE NEUROSIS IN FEMALE DEVELOPMENT. Phyllis Tyson, Ph.D.

Before introducing Dr. Phyllis Tyson, Dr. Henry Smith discussed the current psychoanalytic dialogue on female development. Referring to Elisabeth Young-Bruehl, biographer of Anna Freud, he noted that both Young-Bruehl and Dr. Tyson have argued for a plurality of perspectives regarding female development. They, among others, have attempted to re-examine Freud's views of women in the light of his later theories. Dr. Smith posed questions about the complexity and challenges involved in the study of women, asking, "What is the optimal methodology? How do we as clinicians translate new observations or changes in theory from one frame of reference [to] the psychoanalytic consulting room which generates its own particular observational data?" Dr. Smith praised Dr. Tyson for basing her revision of the theory of female development on her clinical observations.

In her presentation, Dr. Tyson argued that the infantile neurosis central to Freudian structural theory constitutes the structural basis for later adult neurosis. She described the infantile neurosis as an intrapsychic organization characterized by "1) an internalized superego, the functioning of which implies internalized conflict so that drive urges arouse anxiety, and 2) an ego structure which is capable of responding to the anxiety signal with internal modification so that appropriate defense and compromise are responses to the anxiety signal." She suggested that castration anxiety may not be the central motivator for superego formation in women. Anxieties caused by fear of object loss and loss of love lead to conflict and compromise at this stage. Issues of gender identity, narcissism, and self-esteem are closely tied to superego development. The ability to make selective identifications with an ideally viewed mother depends upon internalization, compromise, and defense in order to resolve painful negative feelings. When compromise and internal modification are possible, there is a structural shift in the ego which enables the little girl to maintain an inner sense of the mother as a constant libidinal object, and paves the way toward oedipal progression. As the conflicts of the infantile genital phase are confronted, conflict resolution (or regression or deviation) depends upon the girl's ability (or inability) to utilize the signal function of anxiety. And with the maturational push to the infantile genital phase of development, the girl's task is one of consolidating a narcissistically valued sense of femininity and a female gender role. Noting that penis envy may be a clinical phenomenon during this developmental phase, Tyson stated, "It is not bedrock, nor is it derived from a sense of primary masculinity, nor is it an obligatory aspect of every girl's development. It may be but one among many possible themes and may have any number of underlying meanings.

The Use of an Audiotaped Analysis in a Continuous Case Seminar

Joyce Karp M.D. , Irene Hyler M.D. , Marla Wald M.D. , Laura Whitman M.D. , Samuel Herschkowitz M.D. and Marianne Goldberger M.D.

Marianne Goldberger

Joyce Gerdis Karp, M.D.
155 East 29th St., #30J
New York, NY 10016
Irene Hyler, M.D.
Marla Wald, M.D.
Laura Whitman, M.D.
Samuel Herschkowitz, M.D.
Marianne Goldberger, M.D.

Marianne Goldberger  

ABSTRACT

The use of an audiotaped analysis in a continuous case seminar is evaluated. We compare this case seminar to the traditional one in which an analyst presents process notes, and find that the use of the tape lends itself readily to teaching microanalysis, principles of technique, and observation of affect. Listening to anonymous taped sessions allowed for the possibility of a freer climate for discussion, as none of the seminar participants had a personal relationship with the taped analyst. The disadvantages posed by the absence of the analyst during the seminar also are addressed.

[[RunningHead]]

The Prisonhouse of Psychoanalysis

By Arnold Goldberg. Hillsdale, NJ/London: The Analytic Press, 1990. 175 pp.

Stanley Coen

Stanley Coen

Stanley J. Coen
NEW YORK

Stanley Coen  

Goldberg proposes to question the unexamined foundations of psychoanalysis. Scholars in most disciplines have been questioning the foundations of their field, demonstrating that issues of belief, bias, influence, and power may determine our basic assumptions. Not that such revisionist re-examination is free from these issues of belief, bias, influence, and power. Of course, in our post-structuralist view, all our examinations and re-examinations will be influenced by such motives. For one example, when feminist historians critique male-centered historiography, they not only want to demonstrate that history needs to consider the role of women. They also want to stake their own (feminist) claim that their approach to historical study should be valued as highly as what has been traditional. Such writers have discovered that to make their mark within their discipline, they need to revise the theory of historical study.1

Arnold Goldberg, as a psychoanalyst, also knows this and knows this more immediately than the historians. But he does not tell us right up front that in writing this book he wants to appropriate a greater influence within traditional psychoanalysis for self psychology. As a result, his project of examining foundational concepts in psychoanalysis becomes subverted by his political aims; his critique is ultimately unsatisfying. This is unfortunate because a thoughtful exploration of the unexamined foundations of every school of psychoanalysis would be welcome indeed.

Goldberg especially wants to demonstrate how rigid we can become when we close ourselves off from curiosity, open inquiry, and ongoing creative efforts toward new integration. We tend to restrict ourselves by idealization and addition to psychoanalytic heroes and their theories. He argues that psychoanalysts' rigid adherence to fixed systems of thought, especially with static, mechanical models, may protect against anxiety and uncertainty. But it forecloses the best kind of open psychoanalytic exploration, with our patients and within ourselves.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Lectures on Klein and Bion

Edited by Robin Anderson. London/New York: Tavistock/Routledge, 1992. 139 pp.

Howard Levine

Howard Levine

Howard B. Levine
BROOKLINE, MA

Howard Levine  

This slim volume grew out of a series of lectures offered to the lay public on contemporary developments in Kleinian psychoanalysis. As noted by Hanna Segal in a brief Foreword, the editor and authors sought to "treat the work of Klein and Bion with respect and integrity; not avoiding what is disturbing and not making superficial or easy what is deep and complex" (p. ix). To achieve their aim, the contributors have amplified theoretical constructs with clinical material, presented so as to allow their audience access to the analyst's experience in the consulting room. The result is a well-written collection of essays that illuminate how Kleinian analysts think and work, one that should prove worthwhile and interesting to students and graduate analysts alike.

In nine short chapters, six devoted primarily to Klein and three to Bion, the contributors—Patricia Daniel, Irma Brenman Pick, Ronald Britton, John Steiner, Elizabeth Bott Spillius, Michael Feldman, Edna O'Shaughnessy, and Ruth Riesenberg Malcolm—have crafted a "sampler" that touches upon many of the most interesting and, for the American-trained analyst, perplexing aspects of contemporary Kleinian thinking. Central issues in Kleinian theory are addressed in the book. One involves the fundamental importance and meaning of "unconscious phantasy," a bridge concept between the biology of drive and the psychology of its representation in the mind that is fundamental to the Kleinian conceptualization of character and of transference. Also presented are clinically illustrated explications of the "depressive and paranoid-schizoid positions." Especially emphasized are the fluid and dynamic relationship that is seen to exist between them in the clinical hour and the intimate connection that is seen to exist between the depressive position and the oedipus complex. Another issue addressed is "projective identification" and its relation to thinking, knowing, and being known, which are viewed as fundamental motivational forces in human relations. When their development goes awry, we are told, conflicts arise that can lead to schizoid withdrawal or to frank psychosis.

When a Baby Dies: Psychotherapy for Pregnancy and Newborn Loss

By Irving G. Leon. Foreword by Erna Furman. New Haven/London: Yale University Press, 1990. 230 pp.

Dinora Pines

Dinora Pines

Dinora Pines
LONDON

Dinora Pines  

Leon's book is based upon his work with a clinical sample of forty cases in which perinatal loss was the main focus of his therapeutic endeavor. It is the first book on this topic, and the related literature has been extensively researched. Although Leon discusses miscarriage, abortion, and stillbirth as different aspects of perinatal loss, the stage to which the fetus has matured before the loss has a vital part to play. Perinatal loss at a time when the pregnant woman has felt the baby active and moving within her body, and has anticipated its birth and becoming its mother, concerns not only the physical death of the child but also the death of the baby as an active focus in the mother's conscious and unconscious fantasies, hopes, and daydreams. It is a very different experience from loss in earlier stages, when the baby has not been physically felt. The author states that mourning a perinatal loss is very difficult because there is little or no tangible evidence of the child's existence. My clinical experience cannot confirm this. For a woman who has felt full and now has to return to emptiness, the loss of the baby within her is a palpable loss.

In my experience, pregnant women are very aware of the possibilities of life and death for the fetus and are conscious of their own responsibility for its survival.

467

The Psychoanalytic Review. LXXVIII, 1991

The Dynamics of Narcissism in Marriage. Carolynn Maltas. Pp. 567-581.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

The narcissistic dynamics in marriage are examined from intrapsychic and interpersonal perspectives. Behavior in a spouse can be viewed not only as internally motivated, but as "a response to pressure to conform to the other spouse's inner object relations." The interpersonal viewpoint can illuminate where the intrapsychic cannot. Maltas details three narcissistic marriage styles: 1) a marriage uniting the autonomous and the dependent selves; 2) a marriage uniting the grandiose and devalued selves; and 3) a marriage uniting the indulged and deprived selves.

A Comparative Study of Japanese and American Group Dynamics. Tetsuro Takahashi. Pp. 49-62.

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey

William Jeffrey  

In spite of increased general interest in Japanese groups, little has been written from a psychoanalytic viewpoint. The author uses the model of Bion's concept of the basic assumption group in relation to a work group. He postulates that belonging to a group is a Winnicottian "illusionary experience," i.e., internal reality is felt to perfectly meet external collective reality. Takahashi examines aspects of American and Japanese groups and concludes that Japanese groups "have a high capacity to accommodate this type of illusion, to contain and process fears, and to enrich the group life by bridging the gap between the internal and external reality.

On the Sense of Absence: A Perspective on Womanly Issues

Lila Kalinich M.D.

Lila Kalinich

Lila J. Kalinich, M.D.
300 Central Park West, 1K
New York, NY 10024

Lila Kalinich  

ABSTRACT

Many women express complaints about their mental capacities which are discordant with objective indicators of superior intelligence and functioning. They find their memories unreliable, for example, despite intense efforts to retain facts or ideas. Using clinical material, the author attempts to elucidate how psychic representation of the vagina can contribute to a sense of mental defectiveness, experienced by certain women as peculiarly feminine. The role of such a psychic representation tends to go unrecognized, given that the female genital is usually conceptualized as an "absence" rather than a presence in its own right.

[[RunningHead]]

The Facilitating Environment: Clinical Applications of Winnicott's Theory

Edited by M. Gerard Fromm, Ph.D. and Bruce Lazar Smith, Ph.D. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, Inc., 1989. 673 pp.

F. Rodman

F. Rodman

F. Robert Rodman
BEVERLY HILLS, CA

F. Rodman  

This book adds to an expanding literature about the work of one who, because he sought to disciples, had to be discovered by others. Until recently, there was a certain camaraderie among those who had done so, but the multiplying number of conferences and books (such as the one under review) are turning him into the center of a school, with all the accompanying pitfalls both of idealization and of derision.

The title puts the emphasis on the environmental half of Winnicott's 1965 book, The Maturational Processes and the Facilitating Environment. Because he insisted on the importance of the environment, he was and sometimes still is characterized as one who had lost hold of the vital intrapsychic fountainhead of psychoanalysis as Freud conceived it. I have heard this destructive misreading put forth by analysts who would know better if they cared to read the words that Winnicott wrote. The term "object relations school" is often used not simply as a convenient category of reference, but also to crush out awareness of individual differences among its "members" (there is no organization of object relationists), and to form thereby a convenient category to condemn. Winnicott did not abandon the instincts, ever, as the first chapter of this book (by M. Gerard Fromm) makes clear. But he also believed that a human being is not conceivable outside an interpersonal setting. When he insisted that "there is no such thing as a baby," he was speaking of the omnipresence of the mother. However we formulate our conceptions of the first six months of life, would any of us now disagree?

The book is divided into four sections, a theoretical one concerned with placing him in context, and three others that deal with clinical issues.

On Beginning an Analysis

Edited by Theodore J. Jacobs, M.D. and Arnold Rothstein, M.D. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, Inc., 1990. 309 pp.

Paul Dewald

Paul Dewald

Paul A. Dewald
ST. LOUIS

Paul Dewald  

Attempts to offer psychoanalytic treatment to patients previously considered unsuitable make Freud's aphorism of the opening of a chess game no longer applicable. This collection of papers offers a varied and current assessment of the issues and problems of beginning an analysis. They emphasize the discrepancy between "what candidate analysts are taught (and/or wish to believe) and what

642

experienced graduate analysts actually do in their practices. This discrepancy derives in part from an exclusive emphasis on interpretation and insight in conceptions of analytic process and mode of therapeutic action, as well as corollary aversion for considering what else, in addition to interpretation, takes place in well conducted analyses. The seemingly interminable search for the good analysand with whom the candidate analyst can employ an uncontaminated analytic model contributes to an inhibition to many colleagues' efforts to begin analyses and develop analytic practices" (p. 273).

In Part I, Henry Bachrach summarizes research studies on analyzability. Analyzability and ultimate outcome are extremely difficult to predict at the beginning. Although most patients for whom analysis appears indicated will derive therapeutic benefit, only half will undergo a full analytic process. Only after termination can the analysand be effectively evaluated as to whether he or she was analyzable.

Morton and Estelle Shane emphasize a developmental approach to analyzability and the initiation of an analytic process. The analyst seeks to meet the patient at the arrested level of function and anticipates that the new experience with the analyst will stimulate and protect development of previously arrested capacities. They present a patient for whom it was necessary for the analyst to spend four months serving as a selfobject for the patient's capacity to strengthen her own sense of identity and selfhood. They maintain that this phase of analytic experience was necessary to enable the patient to begin to enter an analysis, given the patient's arrested and skewed development.

The authors propose an approach for gathering information with which to make "an empirical assessment of shifting from psychotherapy to psychoanalysis." Several practical questions need to be asked, including: the rationale for starting with psychotherapy, the kind of psychotherapy techniques used, the basis for the shift to psychoanalysis, the effect of the previous therapy on the opening phase, and the effect of the total experience. The Psychoanalytic Study of Society. XV, 1990

Don't Let the Piranha Bite Your Liver: A Combined Anthropological and Psychoanalytic Approach to Kagwahiv (Tupi) Food Taboos. Waud H. Kracke. Pp. 205-246.

John Hartman

John Hartman

John Hartman  

This study focuses on the food taboos of the Amazonian Kagwahiv culture of Brazil. Contact with whites led to the abandonment of many rituals and beliefs. The

692

tenacity of the food avoidance practices is understood in terms of the deep personal needs of those who hold them. Kracke views the taboos as a multiply determined code which has moral, social status, interpersonal, and parent-child functions. They offer a ritual means for the working out of conflicts arising from destructive as well as sexual wishes. As such, this cultural belief system integrates the demands of the fantasy life of the individual with the requirements of social existence in the group. Individuals use rituals to formulate and restructure their own conflicts.

The Word "Just": An Essay on Resistance, Words, and Multiple Meanings

Vann Spruiell M.D.

Vann Spruiell

Vann Spruiell, M.D.
215 Iona St.
Metairie, LA 70005

Vann Spruiell  

ABSTRACT

This is an essay on the word, just, often used by patients as an ordinary trivial word but also as part of resistance functioning to derail further associations. But there are other, more weighty meanings of the word connected with justice and fairness, and thus, ethics and morality. Besides these, there are hidden meanings that certain words can convey consciously and unconsciously. "Just" is part of a "family" of words, some now obsolete, that range from aspects of law to various passionate derivatives of sexuality and aggression. Therefore, the word, just, can serve as an example to which the insights of psychoanalysis can be applied when seeking answers to questions about the origins, hidden meanings, changes, and apparent losses of meaning of other "ordinary" words.

Stephen Mitchell  

ABSTRACT

Discussions of aggression in the psychoanalytic literature are dominated, both explicitly and implicitly, by loyalty to, or rejection of, Freud's theory of the aggressive drive, which has caused an unfortunate polarization. An approach to aggression is presented that preserves essential features of both drive theory and nondrive theory traditions. It is suggested that this way of thinking about aggression is actually prevalent in both contemporary Freudian and non-Freudian thought without being recognized as such.

The Perverse Attitude Toward Reality

Lee Grossman M.D.

Lee Grossman

Lee Grossman, M.D.
2041 Bancroft Way, Suite 310
Berkeley, CA 94704

Lee Grossman  

ABSTRACT

Freud's (1940a) tentative distinction between the defensive maneuvers in neurosis and those in perversion can be extended to good clinical effect. In general, neurotic defenses may be thought of as directed against wishes, whereas perverse defenses are directed against perceived reality. It is suggested that the perverse approach to reality is not limited to frank sexual perversions; it defines a class of operations that involve taking certain liberties with reality. Clinical material is used to demonstrate the perverse attitude and some of its implications for technique. The role of the superego is considered.

Fred Pine  

ABSTRACT

The place of analyst-patient interactions in the psychoanalytic change process is much debated. This paper reflects an attempt to identify quite specific relational impacts that flow from the requirements of the psychoanalytic situation itself and are (a) essential to the psychoanalytic process, (b) inseparably tied to interpretation, and (c) of quite broad significance. Relationship factors that are idiosyncratic, iatrogenic, or that involve a nonspecific benign tone are all discussed by way of contrast to features seen as essential to the interpretive process. The published literature is heavily used to develop these points.

"Bright Spot," a Variant of "Blind Spot"

Marianne Goldberger M.D.

Marianne Goldberger

Marianne Goldberger, M.D.
1130 Park Ave.
New York, NY 10128

Marianne Goldberger  

The idea of "blind spots" in the analyst has long been a subject of discussion. "Bright spots" for the analyst, on the other hand, have not been described or discussed before. I use the term "bright spot" to indicate a subject that has especially vivid meaning for the analyst and is endowed with rich associative elaborations based on readily available personal experience. When a patient talks about such a subject, the analyst has the feeling that he or she knows in detail exactly what the patient means. Because this feeling may be illusory, a bright spot may prevent adequate analytic exploration.

My introduction to the idea of bright spots occurred at the time of finishing analytic training.1 During a consultation about an analytic patient, I related one analytic hour in which the patient talked about her college experiences. She referred to the fact that those years had not been very good ones for her, which was well known to us, and I mentioned to my supervisor that there developed the usual flavor of low self-esteem connected with this subject, mostly having to do with the academic pressures of that place. He asked if there had been more details about the college experiences, and I responded that as it happened I knew very well exactly what she meant, since I had attended the same college and my own experiences there were still vivid for me. He pointed out that this was a bright spot for me, and that perhaps I was not listening with my customary attention.

1I want to thank Dr. Paul Gray for introducing me to the idea of "bright spots."270

Glen Gabbard

Glen O. Gabbard, M.D.
The Menninger Clinic
Box 829
Topeka, KS 66601-0829

Glen Gabbard  

ABSTRACT

Among the many reasons that feelings of hate develop in love relationships is the need to find and to exaggerate differences in order to maintain a sense of separateness. Freud's notion of the "narcissism of minor differences" provides a framework within which to understand this need to find disappointing differences in one's beloved. Developmental antecedents of this concern about defining and preserving one's separateness can be identified in both oedipal and preoedipal periods.

American Imago. XLVIII, 1991

The Intrusive Past: The Flexibility of Memory and the Engraving of Trauma. Bessel A. van der Kolk and Onno van der Hart. Pp. 425-454.

Sybil Ginsburg

Sybil Ginsburg

Sybil Ginsburg  

The current controversy over the importance of real trauma in causing psychopathology has stimulated interest in the nature of memory. Pierre Janet, a contemporary of Freud to whom the latter acknowledged a debt, differentiated narrative and traumatic memories, coined the term "subconscious," and theorized about the mechanisms resulting in dissociation. His work, including a case history, is discussed in this paper. The authors trace "Freud's ambivalent position vis-à-vis trauma and dissociation" from his original belief in the seduction theory to its repudiation as the concepts of repression and the oedipal conflict were elucidated. At times, however, Freud continued to use the term "repression" to mean "dissociated traumatic memories." Hence the issue has become quite confused. The current distinction between "vertical" and "horizontal" repression is noted. Recent thinking about memory processing, freezing, and triggering are discussed from both psychological and neurobiological viewpoints. The authors note that experience must be acted upon to be integrated, citing Oliver Sack's Awakenings to illustrate this point. While psychoanalysis has, in the past, focused on the examination of psychic reality, neuroscience and psychiatry are "beginning to rediscover" how real trauma is "encoded in memory." Janet is credited with presaging the current work, stating that traumatized persons suffer "from a phobia for the traumatic memory." The difficulty of bridging the world of trauma to "current, ordinary life" is discussed. Finally, the authors speculate about potential ethical treatments for traumatized individuals.

By Albrecht Hirschmüller. New York/London: New York University Press, 1989. 514 pp.

Mary Di

Mary Di

Mary V. Di Gangi
NEW YORK

Mary Di  

This volume by Albrecht Hirschmüller was originally published in German in 1978. It was based on the author's doctoral dissertation for the Institute of the History of Medicine at the University of Tübingen. The book's strength is that it is an extensive and excellent resource of information for the serious scholar interested in the history of science. In a total of 514 pages, there are 93 pages of footnotes, 114 pages of letters and documents, and 71 pages of bibliography. The 206 pages of text are highly condensed, requiring the reader to make continual reference to the source material.

Extremely comprehensive, this book is also the only biography of Breuer published in English. Breuer's life and his intellectual and research interests are discussed in terms of his involvement with the important philosophical and medical issues of nineteenth century Europe. His work in physiology is extensively detailed. It is presented against the background of the prevailing and competing scientific theories of the time.

For the psychoanalytic reader, the book's value is primarily informational. Hirschmüller discusses how Breuer's scientific work and theoretical ideas in physiology informed his contributions to Studies on Hysteria. The 1882 Kreuzlingen report of Breuer's treatment of Anna O is presented for the first time in its entirety. This fourteen-page report by Breuer was written during and immediately after Anna O's treatment at the Bellevue Sanitorium in Kreuzlingen from July 12 to October 29, 1881. The report discusses the detailed development of her symptoms and her morphine addiction. It provides more explicit history about family members than was available before. The interested reader can compare and contrast the account with the discussion Breuer wrote for Studies on Hysteria.

Green asks, can one attribute to an affect the function of representation? And if such a function exists, how can it be integrated into the psychoanalytic concepts of the psyche? In philosophical parlance a representation is a conscious phenomenon, the fact of representing an object to oneself. However, when Freud speaks of unconscious representation, he refers to the mnemic trace of the representation, which, once recathected by a quantum of affect, re-evokes the representation to consciousness. How are we to understand memory traces? Habitually, primary process supports a very partial retention of energy in the memory trace. In the Project for a Scientific Psychology, a memory trace is not a miniaturization of the object, but is described rather as a particular arrangement of facilitation ensuring that, once recathected, this pathway will be utilized rather than another.

Can one speak of a mnemic trace of affect? In the Project Freud speaks of a motor image of discharge, while in 1900 in The Interpretation of Dreams, Freud speaks of the lack of sensorial qualities to the mnemic traces. In Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety of 1926 Freud speaks of affects being incorporated into psychic life through sediments of very archaic traumatic events. Does representation come to be differentiated beginning with this archaic phenomenon apparently older than affect? Or do representations and affect come from the same source? Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences. XXVII, 1991

Wittgenstein on Köhler and Gestalt Psychology: A Critique. Nicholas Pastore, pp. 341-351.

Wittgenstein's objections to Köhler and gestalt psychology are critically examined. Principal features of Köhler's Gestalt Psychology are discussed that are relevant to Wittgenstein's views. They include Köhler's concepts of "subjective" and "objective" experiences, "sensory organization," and "empiristic theory." Wittgenstein's objections, which focus on the concept of sensory organization, are examined. Wittgenstein employs the term "aspect," which is derived from the findings of gestalt psychology, as a replacement for Köhler's term "sensory organization." After his uses of aspect are traced, it is shown that aspect is a superordinate entity distinct from "sensory content" (colors and shapes). This dualism of aspect and sensory content is of the same kind that prevailed in the empiristic theory of visual perception. Wittgenstein's adherence to the empiristic theory is discussed. Finally, the difference between Wittgenstein's aspect and Köhler's sensory organization is examined.

178

Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences. XXVII, 1991

Psychiatry, Psychoanalysis, and Politics During the First World War. José Brunner. Pp. 352-363.

This article compares the therapeutic power used by psychiatrists and psychoanalysts serving in the German and Austro-Hungarian armies during World War I, and the ways in which their therapeutic techniques were related to governmental and military authority. When treating "shell shocked" soldiers, army psychiatrists were guided by nationalist commitment rather than concern for their patients. Whatever theoretical approach they took, they defined their therapeutic task as administrative intervention aimed to increase the docility of soldiers to the state and its military purposes. But violent means of coercion, designed to force neurotic soldiers back into duty, remained inefficient. Drawing from an alternative body of knowledge, army physicians influenced by Freud's writings, or trained in psychoanalysis, applied cathartic methods to treat the Central Power's soldiers. Their approach was not only more humane, but also proved to be therapeutically more efficient.

178

By Andrew B. Druck, Ph.D. Northvale, NJ/London: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1989. 422 pp.

Gerald Adler

Gerald Adler

Gerald Adler
BOSTON

Gerald Adler  

Andrew Druck has written a book that attempts to present four different approaches to the treatment of borderline patients, and to provide the therapist with an understanding of the value of each approach for a specific patient. In many ways he succeeds admirably, outlining a series of useful frameworks and their clinical applications, and relating them to a literature that expands our understanding of work with these patients. Although he describes the four approaches in sufficient detail, a major emphasis of his book is the explication of Kernberg's theoretical and clinical work, since Kernberg has been the major contributor to the borderline personality disorder literature in over the past two decades.

Druck views these models from the vantage point of the primary etiology of the borderline patient's psychopathology as well as of the kind of patient treated, the role of interpretation and confrontation in the treatment, the stance of the therapist, how resistance is understood, and a description of the course of treatment. The four models defined (using Druck's labels) are: (1) Kernberg's model; (2) the representational-deficit, self-deficit model, utilizing the contributions of Buie and Adler, Kohut, and Stolorow; (3) the ego-deficit model, illustrated by the work of Blanck and Blanck; and (4) modifications of classical technique, largely from the writings of Abend, Porder, and Willick.

There are also thoughtful discussions about the use and misuse of transitional objects, from both a theoretical and a clinical vantage point. Particularly valuable are Druck's explorations of the differences in psychoanalytic stances in working with borderline patients in contrast to neurotic patients, in which he synthesizes the work of Eissler, Langs, and Stone.

Why Emotions Can't Be Unconscious: An Exploration of Freud's Essentialism. Jerome C. Wakefield. Pp. 29-67.

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar  

Wakefield views Freud's theory that emotions cannot be unconscious not as an arbitrary semantic exercise, but rather as a way to protect two of his fundamental ideas. The first idea is that unconscious mental states exist, and the second, that the pathogen behind all neurotic symptoms is the patient's sexual instincts. The author tries to shed light on the "essentialistic nature" of Freud's theories, why his theory of emotions remained undeveloped, and the cognitive nature of Freud's approach to the mind. Wakefield's analysis relies on recent philosophical views regarding scientific concepts which distinguish meaning from essence. Freud believed that the essence of an emotion was that it was discharged instinctual energy which was perceived as a feeling. Suppressed emotion could not be unconscious because in the suppressed state it would merely be instinctual energy and thus have no property that would identify it as emotion, or any specific emotion. Also, for Freud, the characteristic that made anything mental was its representability. Bodily discharge which is not perceived is therefore not mental because it has not achieved representation. According to Wakefield, the nature of Freud's thinking about the mind is commensurate with a modern cognitivist view of mental processes dominant in academic psychology at this time.

Adoption and Identity: A Case Study. Ruth Lord and Catherine E. Cox. Pp. 355-368.

The first study is based on psychoanalytically oriented therapy with two groups of adopted child patients, to see what, if any, differences there might be between those adopted at birth (nine children) and those adopted after age two, subsequent to separation from their biological families (eleven children). All twenty children, aged five to thirteen, shared a common posture of rejection toward their adoptive parents and a wish for reunification with their biological parents. However, the fantasies and motives were very different.

The early-adopted children proved to have an intense primary, ambivalent tie to their adoptive parents, although with many anxious fantasies of being defective and rejectable. Their own rejection of the adoptive parents and idealization of their biological parents was thus a defensive, retaliatory move. These children made no actual attempt to find the biological parents. On the other hand, the late-adopted children's tie was still to the biological parents and they did eventually seek them out (though often with disillusioning results). Their relationship to the adoptive parents was more limited, bland, and compliant, secondary to their crusade to find their original parents.

Shelley's novel Frankenstein incorporates uncanny primitive fantasies in a mixture of the naïve and the sophisticated. It can be understood as Shelley's response to her personal history, expressing pathological mourning and attempts at self-reparation. The author, exploring themes of self-disassociation, family romance, pregnancy, and motherhood, emphasizes Shelley's "uneasy awareness of social constraints that rendered any woman's 'masculine' achievements a Promethean act of hubris or a monstrous anomaly." Pregnancy and writing can be creative attempts to repair broken relationships and replace losses. Waites concludes that writing was not a successful solution to Shelley's conflicts, and that she resorted to more conventional solutions—pregnancy and domesticity.

The choice of title for this volume is designed to provoke interest; its content proves to be both controversial and political. The implied promise that "master clinicians" will demonstrate their methods of treating very regressed patients is bound to excite the interest of all psychoanalysts who strive to understand the extent of the regression that is compatible with and necessary for a successful psychoanalysis. Through a Kohutian Lens: William James and Josiah Royce. Vivian M. Rosenberg. Pp. 271-302.

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin

Thomas Acklin  

Using the self psychology of Heinz Kohut, Rosenberg seeks to explore family relationships and the emotional and intellectual lives of two American thinkers. Considering

346

James to have focused more on the freedom and autonomy of the individual, Rosenberg examines Royce's emphasis upon crucial social bonds in family and community. Exploring such Kohutian processes as mirroring leading to healthy narcissism, empathic failures and successes, and various selfobject functions, Rosenberg distinguishes forms of healthy and unhealthy dependencies in the relationships of Royce and James to their parents. James is portrayed as so intensely enmeshed in his family that he needed to extricate himself by establishing autonomy; whereas Royce missed strong relationships and focused on human connectedness in his loneliness. Thus Royce came to appreciate the dependence of human selfhood upon intersubjective relationships, and James came to celebrate individualism. Rosenberg concludes that James's romantic glorification of the individual is less relevant for today than Royce's emphasis on the need for empathy and community.

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar

In examining Schreber's memoirs, Saks explores a theme she says was overlooked by Freud, but was first revealed by White: the child's jealous possessiveness of the parent. Freud's primary emphasis in understanding the etiology of Schreber's illness was his repressed passive homosexual strivings toward his father which created such inner conflict that he fell ill. While Saks agrees that this theme is important, she feels it does not adequately explain much of the memoir. Using the possessiveness theme, Saks discusses Schreber's description of his irresistible pull on God, finally holding God fast, to the exclusion and even death of all possible rivals, all mankind. Soul murder—the complete destruction of Schreber's mental integrity—was attempted on him by Flechsig, who wished to have God all to himself (a projection), and by God, who was attempting to break Schreber's hold on him out of fear that God himself would be destroyed by being possessed by Schreber.

Psychoanalysis and Contemporary Thought. XIV, 1991

Temporality and the Self: A Phenomenological Study of the Narcissist, the Schizoid, and the As-If Personality. Shira Nayman. Pp. 479-503.

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar  

After exploring some philosophical ideas about time, the author wonders how time weaves itself into the fabric of selfhood. Nayman examines the contrasting experience of lived time for three different types of personality disorders, all marked by problems of the self: the narcissistic, the as-if, and the schizoid personalities. The thesis of this paper is that individuals with these disorders have a sense of self that is related to the perspective of time dominating their experience. Further, the author suggests that whether individuals feel they have a self or not depends on how they live in time. The mood tone of these types—the nostalgia of the narcissist, the disembodied hope of the as-if, and the futility of the schizoid—expresses their characteristic rootedness in time. Nayman begins the discussion with Lacan's concepts of lack, absence, and the missed encounter, of how they challenge the self's sense of wholeness and lead to a yearning to return to some lost primordial harmony. The discussion elaborates on the use of nostalgia by narcissists, and how this focus on the past creates the sense of being fraudulent. As-if personalities, on the other hand, are seen as being unsure of their very existence. They frantically search for objects of identification in the mistaken supposition that because they feel so empty, some phenomenon must exist to fill them up. This idea of a future in which they imagine a substantial self is constantly anticipated. In contrast to these first two personality types, schizoids cut off both past and future and are rooted in the present. Schizoids believe that the self never was and never will be, and so are plagued by devitalization and alienation.

This paper illustrates some of the ways in which money and its meanings are important in psychotherapy and psychoanalysis. In American culture candid discussion of money is constrained and converges with individual meanings. Krueger uses clinical vignettes to describe money as symbol and as reality, as well as developmental models and identification involving money. Psychodynamic Psychotherapy of Borderline Patients

By Otto F. Kernberg, M.D., Michael A. Selzer, M.D., Harold W. Koenigsberg, M.D., Arthur C. Carr, Ph.D., and Ann H. Appelbaum, M.D. New York: Basic Books, Inc., 1989. 210 pp.

Gerald Adler

Gerald Adler

Gerald Adler
BOSTON

Gerald Adler  

This succinct and clearly written book is a welcome addition to the understanding and treatment of borderline patients. The authors have provided an articulate statement of Kernberg's theoretical and treatment framework, and have used their wisdom both to add to it and to make it understandable for a wide audience. Although they caution the reader that this primer may present ideas and treatment implications in a way that is too much in outline form, they do provide a thoughtful and well-balanced account of Kernberg's and The New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center, Westchester Division's, view of the expressive psychotherapy of borderline personality disorder patients.

The authors emphasize that their treatment approach is based on a view of borderline patients as individuals who have a stable, pathological internal world in which the major ways of coping with significant childhood frustration and/or excessive, pathological aggression is through the use of the major defenses of splitting, projective identification, primitive idealization, and denial. They contrast their view of borderline patients with those in the neurotic spectrum and outline the treatment implications of these distinctions. They define the core of their approach as the analysis of splitting, which requires clarification and confrontation in order to prepare the patient for the interpretation of splitting, an essential ingredient of the expressive psychotherapy they elaborate. They also emphasize the use of countertransference to help the therapist understand the process of splitting and projective identification that has occurred, now involving the therapist.

Especially useful for the clinician are the rich clinical illustrations which make their theoretical formulations and clinical advice come alive. These vignettes, often presented as verbatim interactions between patient and therapist, are vivid examples of therapists in action, processing countertransference awareness of projective identifications, which they use to interpret the complex projective identification and splitting processes to the patient.

An Unusual Relationship: The Final Encounter of Picasso and Matisse

Milton Viederman M.D.

Milton Viederman

Milton Viederman, M.D.
New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Ctr.
525 East 68 St.
New York, NY 10021

Milton Viederman  

ABSTRACT

Picasso and Matisse renewed their relationship in 1946 as the aging Matisse approached death. Picasso, ordinarily contemptuous of others and indifferent to their needs, revealed a markedly different attitude toward Matisse, whom he admired and whose affection and approbation he sought. The roots of Picasso's attitude are traced to his morbid concern about bodily deterioration and fear of death. Matisse, apparently serene in his confrontation with approaching death, represented an ideal to Picasso, a hoped-for remedy for anxiety, a confident paternal representation so unlike his father. Freud's view of death, poetically expressed in his paper, "On Transience," is a model for contrasting Picasso's "revolt … against mourning" with Matisse's sense of symbolic immortality.

Gerard Fountain  

Milrod presents an excellent, clear, and interesting review of the notion of the ego ideal. He discusses its relation to the superego and refutes some other writers' views of its nature. He explains its detachment from the personified "idols" and its gradual removal from such personified early love objects. He notes four stages in formation of the ego ideal and its relation to the wished-for self-image. The superego may be described as measuring the praise or blame to assign to the ego. Milrod discusses the ego ideal as it relates to group formation: the group enables its members to ignore their ego ideals. He has some tantalizingly brief remarks—one hopes he will later elaborate—on the ego ideal in the psychopath and on the origin of the double, contradictory, ego ideal found in some persons. His remarks on the meaning and origin of guilt and shame are also brief but stimulating. Some brief case discussions well illustrate what Milrod has to say. There is much more in this essay than can be included in a brief summary.

Christiane Olivier, identified on the dust jacket only as "an analyst in Aix-en-Provence," has written a mostly polemical but ultimately timely book exploring the effect of mothers on their children. With the postmodern insistence on the rootedness of all knowledge in culture and history and the widespread skepticism about the possibility of any universal theories of human nature and culture, it is inevitable that psychoanalysis, which has always prided itself on being as much an intellectual as a clinical discipline, would feel the need to address the issue of its cultural embeddedness. Many psychoanalysts are aware that in the current intellectual climate, the cultural and historical transcendence of their theories can no longer be taken for granted but has to be rigorously demonstrated.

It is therefore with a sense of anticipation that one turns to Roland's book, in which he seeks to compare Western, Indian, and Japanese psyches and thus to examine the question of the relativity of psychoanalytic concepts. The anticipation is enhanced by the claim that the book is based on his clinical experience and that its direct psychoanalytic understanding of patients distinguishes it from other, similar works in the field.

Roland's main conclusion is that "the intrapsychic self varies significantly if not radically according to the social and cultural patterns of societies so civilizationally different. I find that people have a different experiential, affective sense of self and relationships, as well as vastly different internalized world views that give profoundly different meanings to everyday experiences and relationships" (p. 4, italics added). Although I am sympathetic to Roland's intentions, the italicized words in the quotation give me pause. They seem to deny the common humanity of American, Indian, and Japanese patients; and one needs to closely scrutinize Roland's primary data, the case histories, to see how far such a conclusion is justified. This is where the disappointment begins. Roland's patients from India and Japan come across as if they are solely constituted of cultural masks with, at the most, unformed individual faces. We do not get the mythos of a psychoanalytic case history and its conveying of meaning through narrative and the power of aesthetics, making a person come alive in his or her individuality beyond the cultural propositions that seek to define the individual.
