[[RunningHead]]

On the Setting of Analytic Fees

Joan Erle M.D.

Joan Erle

Joan B. Erle, M.D.
120 East 75th St.
New York, NY 10021

Joan Erle  

Among the exceptional features of a psychoanalysis is the requirement of frequent visits over a long period of time. That, of course, entails the payment of a very substantial sum of money. Many patients have limited financial resources. In regard to this issue, it is common to hear references to the need for a "reduced fee." It is the meaning and use of this term—for the analyst and the patient—that I want to discuss.

What does "reduced fee" connote? The implication would seem to be that the analyst has a usual fee—the so-called "full fee"—which he/she is offering to lower for this particular patient.1 It would seem to present the analyst's view of him/herself as a person whose services have a high and specific value. Does it also imply that this patient is so worthwhile and interesting a person that the analyst is willing to make this special arrangement? How does the patient experience this indication of interest or favor? How does the patient deal with the question of whether the analyst would be willing to make this arrangement if the analyst could fill all of his/her time at the "full fee"? The disappointment and the injury to the analyst's feelings of self-worth when appropriate analytic cases are not easily available may contribute to the importance of the term "full fee" and the diminishment reflected in the term "reduced fee."

1I am reminded of an old joke about the man traveling for the first time in a Pullman car who did not know how much to tip the porter. He decided to ask the porter what his average tip was. The porter replied, "Five dollars, sir." (This is a very old joke.) The man gave him five dollars, and the porter broke into a grin, saying, "Thank you, sir, you're the first person who ever came up to my average."106

Jacob Jacobson

Jacob G. Jacobson, M.D.
1636 16th Street
Boulder, CO 80302

Jacob Jacobson  

ABSTRACT

This overview of the therapeutic relationship in psychoanalysis utilizes a sampling of findings of infant observational research to illuminate issues in the evolving technique of psychoanalysis. The therapeutic relationship is followed schematically through the course of a treatment, from initial contact through termination, and the gradual shift of psychoanalytic technique toward an interactional view of the psychoanalytic situation is noted. During the middle phase, some areas of current controversy in psychoanalysis are discussed, along with views on the multiple theoretical models currently available for organizing psychoanalytic data and for gaining clinical access for analytic work.

Arnold Goldberg  

ABSTRACT

This paper is a reconsideration of the role of sexualization in psychoanalysis. After a review of the accepted definitions of sexualization as defense and/or part of normal sexuality, a new explanation is offered. This posits sexualization as a psychological manifestation of a structural deficit and suggests analytic treatment as a process of structuralization. These terms are defined and illustrated. A case example demonstrates the thesis, and some implications of this concept are discussed.

On the Value of Explicit Reconstruction

Gail Reed Ph.D.

Gail Reed

Gail S. Reed, Ph.D.
1199 Park Ave.
New York, NY 10128

Gail Reed  

ABSTRACT

Classical psychoanalysis provides a clinical method and a technique which enable us to help the patient undo primary process transformations of crucial organizing events and the fantasies about them, toward the end of understanding not only the original internal components of conflicts still persisting in the present, but the manner in which the patient originally constructed his or her unique pathogenic system of meaning. That technique involves explicit reconstruction. Private systems of meaning are frequently constructed around the apparently arbitrary contiguities of life, and only the reconstruction of those contiguities can reveal to the patient how he or she has understood and continues to understand the data of external perception. An extended clinical example is presented.

A Screen Memory: My Recollections and Distortions of the 1950 Film, Three Came Home

Herbert Stein M.D.

Herbert Stein

Herbert H. Stein, M.D.
425 East 79th St.
New York, NY 10021

Herbert Stein  

For many years, I had a clear memory that in my childhood my favorite movie, and also the first movie I ever saw, was Three Came Home. I remembered having seen it with my mother when I was four years old. It was about American women who were captured by the Japanese on a Pacific Island and their experience in the Japanese internment camp. I had vague memories of scenes in which the women were abused and beaten by the Japanese. At the end of the film, allied warplanes flew overhead, and the allies retook the island, freeing the women. In the last scene, three soldiers walked up a road, arm in arm, with the middle one missing the lower part of one leg. I thought that they were the husbands of the women being freed.

Because it seemed to have been important to me at one time, I had a good deal of curiosity about the film. It never appeared on television or in the video stores, so I was unable to see it again. A few years ago, I looked it up in a book listing films, which I found in my accountant's waiting room. I don't know exactly what I expected to find, but I think that I was excited and relieved to find a tangible relic of this special childhood memory. The brief description roughly fit my memory, but I was slightly disturbed that the film was listed as having been made in 1950. Since I was born in early 1945, it seemed unlikely I had seen it at four, as I had been firmly convinced. Even then, I thought that perhaps I had seen it at the beginning of the year, or that it had been released early.

I had also always wondered about the title. I assumed it referred to the three returning soldiers. However, the film focused on the women.

K. Arvanitakis M.D. , R. Jodoin , E. Lester , A. Lussier and B. Robertson

B. Robertson

B. Robertson  

ABSTRACT

An examination of the nightmares of four adults in analysis who had been sexually abused as children revealed a characteristic distortion of the body representation as it appeared in the manifest content of the dream. The authors believe that childhood sexual trauma has profound and pervasive effects on the development and consolidation of the body image. Experienced as a grave assault on body integrity and function, it mobilizes primitive anxieties and specific genital anxieties, resulting in distortion, fragmentation, or disintegration of the body representation. The frequently observed multiple somatization of victims of sexual abuse is attributable to such a damaged and persecutory body representation.

Meeting of the Psychoanalytic Association of New York

January 11, 1993. TRANSFERENCE AS A COMPROMISE DEFENSE. Jacob A. Arlow, M.D.

Analysis of the transference remains the central technical imperative of psychoanalysis. Dr. Arlow noted, however, that Freud's conceptualization (in the Introductory Lectures) of the transference neurosis, wherein "the whole of the [patient's] illness's new production is concentrated upon a single point—his relation to the doctor," is extreme by current standards. Although Freud abandoned the term "transference neurosis" after 1922, the tradition of exclusively transference-oriented technique which he established remains influential. Related to this is the assumption that only transference interpretations are mutative. According to Dr. Arlow, these views concerning the primacy of transference interpretation remained relatively unchallenged until Dr. Harold P. Blum's 1983 paper, "The Position and Value of Extratransference Interpretation."

Dr. Arlow noted that his own attention had been drawn to this issue when he observed, in consultation, supervision, and clinical seminars, that at times analysts' exclusive concentration on transference created an "artificial inhumanity" and led to neglect of the material. As he put it, "They are not listening to the material; they are listening for material, transference material." Dr. Arlow stated that the catalyst for his decision to write the current paper came at a workshop at an Annual Meeting of the American Psychoanalytic Association, where he observed that the analyst/presenter had failed to take up painful, affect-laden, and genetically significant material in the session because of exclusive concentration on transference. What troubled him, he said, was that no one in the audience, which included several leading figures in the field, raised the issue that "dealing with the transference … at this time, in this context, was entirely out of place."

The concept of transference, Dr. Arlow emphasized, is rooted in Freud's very concretistic early thinking regarding libidinal cathexes. In Freud's original conception of transference, according to Dr. Arlow, "the cathexis vested in the mental representation of the original, that is, the primary object of the libido, is transferred and becomes vested in the mental representation of the analyst," thus supposedly making in the transference "a living record of the forgotten past." What gets overlooked even today, however, is that "manifest transference constitutes a defensively distorted set of derivative representations of the unconscious conflict as organized into some form of unconscious compromise fantasy." Dr. Arlow described how a recent presenter at a symposium described "transferences [as] manifest, complicated interactions between the patient and a parent that were subsequently repeated with the analyst." Infant Observation and Psychoanalytic Theory

Stephen Seligman

Stephen Seligman

Stephen Seligman, D.M.H.
Department of Psychiatry Infant-Parent Program San Francisco General Hospital University of California, San Francisco
Bldg. 9, Room 130
2550 23rd St.
San Francisco, CA 94110

Stephen Seligman  

The effort to bring infant observation to bear on psychoanalytic theory has been criticized on the basis that we cannot make reliable inferences about an infant's inner world since we lack verbal reports from the infant. Zuriff (1992), for example, has recently argued that data from direct observation of infants cannot be used to alter existing psychoanalytic formulations because of "general logical difficulties in inferring intrapsychic experience from behavioral data in the absence of introspection" (p. 33).

Such criticism overlooks the fact that psychoanalytic theory has always made inferences about infant observation to build theory; inasmuch as this is so, the more recent observationally based approaches are no more speculative than the earlier ones. Freud (1920), in his pivotal interpretation of the famous "Fort-Da" vignette, used inferences about preverbal experience as evidence for the repetition compulsion, a fundamental psychoanalytic concept that remains influential today. Like today's infant researchers, Freud was mindful of the difficulties involved in characterizing infantile psychic life, going so far as to caution his readers that he was drawing on a "fiction" in his early linkage of infancy and primary process (1911, pp. 219-220, n. 4). Nonetheless, he proceeded with the effort, and a number of subsequent analysts have done the same. Many images of the infant have been proposed that have influenced analytic theory and clinical practice: the aggressively fantasizing baby of Melanie Klein and her followers (Isaacs, 1948); (Klein, 1952), the merging infant of Margaret Mahler (Mahler, Pine, Bergman, 1975)

Vincent: The Self-Portraits

W. Meissner S.J.

W. Meissner

W. W. Meissner, S.J.
129 Mount Auburn St.
Cambridge, MA 02138

W. Meissner  

ABSTRACT

The self-portraits of Vincent van Gogh are examined in the context of his tragic life experience, ending in psychosis and suicide. The self-portraits are seen as repeated and unresolved efforts at self-exploration and self-definition in an attempt to add a sense of continuity and cohesion to a fragile and fragmented self-experience. The portraits are painted in mirror perspective; Vincent's search for identity is thus seen as mediated by the dynamics of the mirroring phenomenon. Further implications are explored in terms of processes of projection and introjection and their role in self-consolidation.

James Edgar

James Edgar  

Stolorow feels the discussion about conversion from psychotherapy to psychoanalysis presupposes assumptions about the difference between the two. He discusses four such assumptions (he calls them myths): the myth of the neutral analyst, the myth of interpretation without suggestion, the myth of uncontaminated transference, and the myth of the analyzable (or unanalyzable) patient. He ties neutrality to abstinence and points out that it may not only fail to facilitate analytic work but actually be "inherently inimical" to it. He suggests replacing neutrality with "an attitude of sustained empathic inquiry" and predicts what effect that will have on the analytic process.

Psychoanalytic Theories of Development: An Integration

By Phyllis Tyson, Ph.D. and Robert L. Tyson, M.D. New Haven/London: Yale University Press, 1990. 398 pp.

Alan Zients

Alan Zients

Alan B. Zients
WASHINGTON, DC

Alan Zients  

The Tysons are eminently qualified to accept the challenge of evolving an integration of psychoanalytic developmental theories. They have correctly perceived the need of students for assistance in assimilating in a coherent manner the vast and often contradictory literature on development. Their decision to maintain an intrapsychic focus assists in organizing the diverse theoretical perspectives.

To achieve the integration they are striving for, the authors construct an organizing framework derived from the work of Piaget, Spitz, Anna Freud, and von Bertalanffy. While specific applications of this framework may appear overly reductionistic and somewhat distorting, it does assist in providing a backdrop for understanding the developmental stages. The chart at the end of Chapter Two provides useful assistance in conceptualizing and understanding the authors' correlation of the different developmental sequences throughout the book.

An alternative approach would have been to tell the story of development longitudinally, avoiding the occasionally awkward division into separate systems. This alternative approach might have enabled the reader to obtain a more integrated picture of development at different ages.

To encompass such a rich and rapidly expanding body of knowledge in so few pages, the authors have had to make difficult choices. Major contributions are briefly summarized in a manner that at times does not communicate their full significance or complexity. The degree of acceptance of or doubt about certain contributions is not sufficiently elaborated.

What is Effective in Psychoanalytic Therapy. The Move from Interpretation to Relation

By W. W. Meissner, S.J., M.D. Northvale, NJ/London: Jason Aronson, Inc., 1991. 192 pp.

Edgar Levenson

Edgar Levenson

Edgar A. Levenson
NEW YORK

Edgar Levenson  

It is now commonly agreed that the central issue in both psychoanalytic theory and practice is the shift from the intrapsychic premise of interpretation as providing mutative insight to interpretation as relational participation with the patient; that is, interpretation not as the imparting of truth to the patient about the patient, but rather as an interaction with the patient, since every interpretation is a choice and is necessarily colored by the therapist's participation in the process. This appears as a less radical concept to some analysts than to others; but the orthodox analytic community, as a whole, has been struggling for some years now to integrate quite radical departures from the mutative interpretation view and still maintain the integrity and continuity of the psychoanalytic movement. In order to do so, a narrative of continuity must be created—that interpretation as insight flows logically into interpretation as relationship; otherwise, one might possibly be confronted with a view of the psychoanalytic movement as fragmenting.

To be fair, I must first make my own orientation clear. I am an interpersonal psychoanalyst, affiliated with the William Alanson White Psychoanalytic Institute, which has a long history of interest in the therapist/patient relationship and an equally long history of being outside the fold. There is a very extensive literature on relational psychoanalysis which has been largely unknown to traditional analysts, but it is now beginning to attract attention. Still, it is astonishing to see a book on the move from interpretation to relation contain no reference to current literature, such as Greenberg and Mitchell's book, Object Relations in Psychoanalytic Theory, widely considered a seminal text.1

Meissner is University Professor of Psychoanalysis, Boston College, and Training and Supervising Analyst at the Boston Psychoanalytic Institute; and, as a prominent author and teacher, he is

1Greenberg, J. R. & Mitchell, S. A. (1983): Object Relations in Psychoanalytic Theory. Cambridge: Harvard Univ. Press. A bibliography of that literature would be well beyond the purposes of a review, but a three-volume compendium of interpersonal literature is in press: Interpersonal Theory in Psychoanalysis, edited by M. Lionells, et al., Hillsdale, NJ: Analytic Press.

Dream, Phantasy and Art

By Hanna Segal. London/New York: Tavistock/Routledge, 1991. 120 pp.

Howard Levine

Howard Levine

Howard B. Levine
BROOKLINE, MA

Howard Levine  

In this brief book, Hanna Segal offers readers an eloquent discussion of the centrality of unconscious fantasy to art, imagination, creativity, and the aesthetic response. Along the way, she illuminates many interesting currents of thought in contemporary Kleinian theory and practice, expands her earlier work on dreams, fantasy, and symbolism,1 and discusses and masterfully synthesizes formulations of Freud, Klein, and Bion. As Betty Joseph notes in her Introduction, this book cannot be categorized as only theoretical, clinical, or applied (p. xi). Rather, each of these perspectives is an essential, interconnected component of the book itself.

Segal begins her study with Freud's view of the dream as the "royal road" to the understanding of the unconscious, but quickly moves via Klein to a conception of the unconscious structured by a complex organization of wishes and defenses firmly rooted in object relations. It is the latter, existing from the very beginning of life, which give rise to an inner world of unconscious fantasy that is "the matrix of our mental structure and life" (p. 25). Freud2 saw unconscious fantasy as a relatively late addition to mental functioning that was highly organized, referred mainly to whole objects, and was comparable in structure to dreams, symptoms, and parapraxes. In contrast, Segal (and the Kleinians) views unconscious fantasy as a core, primary activity of the mind; a direct, albeit unconscious, expression of instincts and impulses; a constant and universal phenomenon of psychic functioning that is active from the very start of mental life.

Psyhcoanalysis and Contemporary Thought. XIV, 1991

Early Superego Development: The Emergence of Shame and Narcissistic Affect Regulation in the Practicing Period. Allan N. Schore. Pp. 187-250.

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar

Joel Gonchar  

This paper reviews both the clinical and the research literature on the origins of superego development in the practicing subphase of separation-individuation. Specifically, Schore examines the origin of the superego in its function as an autoregulator of affect. His thesis is that the affect of shame has a critical functional role as it emerges in object relational interactions between caretaker and child in the practicing subphase which leads to these interactions becoming internalized as a shame regulatory system. Further, this system is shown to contribute strongly to the resolution of the crucially important rapprochement crisis. The way in which the system contributes to the ego ideal component of the superego as a mood regulator is presented, as well as how its maldevelopment leads to narcissistic pathology. The literature presented is from psychoanalysis, infant research, developmental psychology, and neurobiology. The latter research presents the data about the underlying neurophysiologic substrate of brain structures and where they are in development during the practicing subphase. The importance of the autonomic nervous system is highlighted, in that the shame regulatory system operates to down-regulate a hyperaroused sympathetic dominated nervous discharge or to up-regulate a hypoaroused para-sympathetic dominated discharge. The importance of this preverbal self-regulatory ego ideal in setting basic mood and affect disposition, as well as self-esteem regulation, is emphasized.

Jahrbuch Der Psychoanalyse. Beiträge Zur Theorie Und Praxis

Band 26. (Yearbook of Psychoanalysis. Contributions to Theory and Practice. Vol. 26.) Stuttgart: Frommann-Holzboog, 1990. 286 pp.

Ernest Wolf

Ernest Wolf

Ernest S. Wolf
WINNETKA, IL

Ernest Wolf  

For many years now the Jahrbuch has brought to the German speaking reader major essays from the world's leading psychoanalysts. This volume, like its predecessors, continues to present quality psychoanalytic contributions concerned with important topics. The authors

647

presented are well-known psychoanalysts from Britain, Germany, Italy, Switzerland, and the United States. They give this book an international flavor, and they acquaint the reader with some of the diverse directions into which psychoanalytic inquiry has moved while maintaining a core psychoanalytic identity.

The eight papers are divided into four sections: theoretical contributions (A. Limentani, D. Chianese, B. Barth, H. Harsch); a clinical contribution (L. Wurmser); applied psychoanalysis (P. Dettmering, E. Haas); and a biographical contribution about Freud (E. Garcia).

Limentani's chapter, "Aggression, Sexuality and the Death Instinct," gives an overview of the development of the psychoanalytic theories as conceptualized primarily by Freud and by M. Klein. He holds Freud's views as presented in the 1915 essay, "Instincts and their Vicissitudes," as still being of great significance for psychoanalysis. Analysts were ill prepared to deal with Freud's introduction in the 1920's of his revolutionary concept of a dichotomy between Eros and Thanatos. It gave the repetition compulsion greater prominence than the pleasure principle. The new theory was not acceptable to many psychoanalysts, although it found clinical support in making the negative therapeutic reaction explainable. Further modifications were inevitable in order to come to grips with the role of the environment and found their expression in object relations theory. Comparing Freudian and Kleinian approaches to describing the interplay of libido and aggression, Limentani seems more attracted to the Kleinian view but is critical of both. He faults all psychoanalytic theorizing as centered too much on pathology and lacking in understanding of normal sexuality. He stresses the importance of excitations. Therefore, inasmuch as excitement is regarded as the essence of sex, it follows that its relation to aggression can be discussed without taking recourse to the death instinct. Finally, Limentani describes his personal clinical approach with a case report that illustrates the interrelationship of sexuality, aggression, and pregenital development.

Richard Almond

Richard Almond  

Tragedy is both central and overlooked in psychoanalysis. It is central because analysis deals with conflict, with the inevitability of disappointment in every analysis and in every hour; it is overlooked because in the offer of treatment we hold out hope that disappointment may be overcome for an outcome that is "better." In our psychoanalytic value system, truth and realism live in tension with the actuality of the analytic relationship—a dyadic bond that speaks to the deepest, most subjective potential in patients.

The Use of the Self. Countertransference and Communication in the Analytic Situation

By Theodore J. Jacobs, M.D. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, Inc., 1991. 237 pp.

Howard Levine

Howard Levine

Howard B. Levine
BROOKLINE, MA

Howard Levine  

In recent years, American psychoanalysts have been involved in a major reconceptualization of the psychoanalytic process. To reiterate the words of Warren Poland, who has contributed a brief but eloquent Foreword to this excellent book, an increasing awareness of the interactive, dyadic dimensions of psychoanalysis has brought us to the point of now being able to consider the analytic process as "a vital interchange between … two participants" (p. xii), in which "the examination of the patient's mind is realized within a matrix of a deeply buried pair of reciprocal self-inquiries" (p. xiii). The papers contained in Theodore Jacobs's new book, The Use of the Self, represent an important contribution to this reconceptualization. It should be of immediate interest and value to every psychoanalytic student, clinician, and clinical theorist.

In Jacobs's experience, the diagnosis and rectification of certain insidious, but significant analytic difficulties require us to carry our investigations beyond "the words exchanged between patient and analyst" (p. xxi) to the hidden messages that underlie these words. These messages, which are frequent, unrecognized accompaniments to the more manifest analytic discourse, can reflect subtle judgments or covert communications of performative intent on the part of either participant in the analytic relationship. Rather than appear in the content of speech, these messages may instead be "transmitted through tone and syntax, vocal quality and inflection, posture and movement" (p. xxi). If these nonverbal channels of experience are not carefully and consistently monitored by the analyst, the impact of the messages that they convey may go unrecognized, and various forms of therapeutic stalemate may ensue. When they are attended to, they can furnish the analyst with a powerful source of data about the analytic relationship, which can be used to inform the analyst's interventions and to free up his/her analyzing instrument from the encumbering limitations of countertransference restrictions.

Estelle Shane
Morton Shane
LOS ANGELES

Morton Shane  

Joseph Lichtenberg's book is a remarkable compendium on psychoanalytic thinking about motivation. In it Lichtenberg offers a reconceptualization of motivation, a modification of psychoanalytic theory that effectively preserves the insights of classical psychoanalysis while bringing them into the wider scientific world of infant and child observers, ethologists, neurophysiologists, and philosophers of science. He is to be applauded because he offers us a theory of motivation that, even if we do not accept it in its entirety, can at least serve as a starting point for consideration and reconsideration.

Of course, Lichtenberg is not alone in suggesting that psychoanalytic motivational theory requires reformulation. Out of numerous examples, we will cite two: Modell,1 who points to well-established conclusions from ethological findings to contend that instinct, as representing a motivational source solely from within, must be reconsidered, that no biological entity can be considered apart from interacting with its environment; and Sandler,2 who suggests that a revision of drive theory is necessary if we are to take into consideration what is known from the consulting room about object relations, asserting that the desire for sexual expression, as pressing as it may be under certain circumstances, is secondary to the need for safety when the individual is threatened with loss of connectedness to the needed object.

[[RunningHead]]

Revue Française De Psychanalyse. XLIX, 1985

The Work of Instinct and of Representation: Thing-Representation and Word-Representation. Alain Gibeault. Pp. 753-772.

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson  

The discovery of the separate destinies of affect and representation led Freud to advance the hypothesis of the unconscious and to elaborate his theory of the psychical or ideational representatives of instinct. This delegation of instinct to representatives is in Freud equally qualified by the contrast between word-presentation and thing-presentation. Dealing with these systems of representation, the author focuses on the theme of word- and thing-presentation in Freud's discussions of the topic, and then broadens the discussion to include the relation between language and primary and secondary process thinking. He concludes with some final remarks on representation, symbolization, and linguistic meaning.

The distinction between word- and thing-presentations dates from Freud's 1891 monograph, On Aphasia. Freud maintains a distinction there between signifier/signified and sign/thing, close to that of Saussure and structural linguistics. Freud thus maintained these two systems of representation: (1) a distinction interior to language, between word-presentation and thing-presentation, and (2) a difference external to language, between thing-presentation and the thing actually in the world. On Aphasia was an attempt to establish a psychology of representations independent of the nervous system, in opposition to his predecessors who had constructed associationist schemata founded on the research on cerebral localization. Freud's language apparatus in the aphasia monograph is the precursor of the psychic apparatus of the psychological works, and his two systems of representation, thing- and word-presentations, constitute an independent order of systems of relations founded on the body or the external world. Freud used this dual system of representations in his distinctions between verbal, asymbolic, and agnosic types of aphasia. The emphasis on presentation rather than sign indicates the importance the monograph placed on the psychological doubling of the word or thing in mnemic images. This reflects what the linguists call the denotative or referential function of signs. Reference and representation cannot be assimilated, as Frege showed in his distinction between Sinn (meaning) and Bedeutung (reference). Representation and reference are distinguished by various contrasts, e.g., between subjective and objective, connotative and denotative, emotional and cognitive, poetic and scientific discourse. Yet for Freud the function of representation participated at the same time in objective denotation and in subjective connotation.

[[RunningHead]]

L'Adolescent Face a Son Corps. (The Adolescent and his Body.)

By Annie Birraux. Paris: Éditions Universitaires, 1990. 180 pp.

Eva Lester

Eva Lester

Eva P. Lester
MONTREAL

Eva Lester  

Social awareness of adolescence as a specific developmental stage between childhood and adulthood appeared (in the West) only at the end of the eighteenth century, following the establishment of compulsory military service, according to Philippe Ariès, the historian of family life. Anthropological studies in the 1930's and '40's have revealed that in preindustrial societies such awareness is still lacking, although the rites of passage, common to all societies and designed to permit the pubertal child to resolve identity conflicts and accept procreative roles, point to the cultural recognition of the significance of pubertal maturation. Using Kafka's Metamorphosis as her central metaphor, Annie Birraux attempts to go beyond what she calls the "banalization" of adolescence by current sociologizing, in order to "rediscover the adolescent … in his intimacy and his dealing with his own pubertal body" (p. 13). The notion itself of adolescence, the author maintains, contains profound and defining bodily changes. Any theoretical approach to this age period must center around the body as it exists and functions in physical and symbolic space and as it experiences desire.

Adolescence is both a specific period, the psychological and sociocultural period of puberty, and a process, that of the psychic integration of the changes introduced in the body by puberty. The sexual body of the adolescent, continuously changing in its external forms and internal representations, becomes the site of "a dialectic between the child's body, known and fantasied … and the unknown, mysterious, sexually mature body of the adolescent …" (p. 17).

Birraux, in her psychoanalytic perspective, not exhaustive but a fitting perspective with which to approach the internal process of adolescence, as she says, is firmly anchored in a "classic" structuraldrive defense model of the mind. She has a strong developmental bias, in that she stresses repeatedly the profound changes in the personality organization which are brought about by this developmental phase. Her expositions are basically not original.
